headline: I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta.
text: I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta . Benchmarks I've found over 6 years: 1. 1 new creative concept per $10k in monthly spend. At $500k/month that's 50 concepts (~3 ads per concept, more for static-heavy). 2. At $100k/mo, aim for 70% new concepts and 30% variations. As you scale past $1m/mo, max out at 50/50. But never drop below 50% new. 3. 70% of your creatives should be cut before week 2. Only 10-20% will ever hit your performance threshold. If you're keeping most of your ads alive, you're probably losing money. 4. Your top 1-2% of ads should drive 50% of total spend. If they don't, you haven't found real winners yet or you haven't utilized them well enough. 5. Big swings have lower hit rates (5-10%) but higher total potential. These are the ads that can scale to $1m+ in spend. 6. 70% video, 30% static for most ecom brands. New brands need more video (more education, less BOF audience). Clothing should lean heavier static (lots of SKUs to show). 7. 15-20% of budget goes to testing. Under 10% and your creative pipeline dries up. Over 25% and you're burning cash without enough scale behind winners. 8. When you 2x spend, expect 20-30% ROAS decline. A $30 CPA at $50k/month might become $40 at $200k. Scale requires better ads, better optimization, better structure, or lower targets. 9. Limit bid and budget changes to 25% max. For 90% of changes, smaller and more frequent changes outperform bigger ones. 10. Meta always targets returning customers. Aim to keep returning conversions under 15-20%. Accept it and plan around it. 11. Ad copy can improve performance up to 50%. But a great ad outperforms by 500%. Copy matters, but the creative itself is where the real leverage is. 12. A great media buyer improves ROAS 100%+ vs a bad one. Creative strategists make better decisions when they're working off clean data and with better media buyers, because the scaled ads are actual winners. Hope this helps. What others have I missed?

headline: I spoke to a Sales leader this week.
text: I spoke to a Sales leader this week. She joined a new company 2 months ago. She's meeting with their existing vendors to evaluate which contracts she'll renew, which ones she'll expand, and which ones she'll cancel. She had 3 renewal convos this week. Guess how many of those convos left her wanting to renew or expand? 0. She works for a large company. Two are 6-figure contracts, one is 5-figures. They're well-known, "AI-pilled" vendors. You've see them on stages talking about how they've optimized their Sales orgs with AI. And, everyone sits in the audience ooh-ing and ahh-ing and thinking, "We better do this, too". And, yet, we don't stop and ask, "Do these tactics make the experience better for the buyer?". Call me a luddite (I've been called a lot worse), but I think the most important quality in a Sales leader operating in this "Look....a squirrel! Look...a squirrel!" AI era we're living is restraint. OpenClaw! Go buy Mac Minis! AI SDRs! Fire the SDRs! Agentforce! Automate everything! Muse! OMG have you tried it?! Instinct! It's changing the game! ChatGPT/Claude! Use it for everything! A Sales leader can't be the talking dog, Doug, from the movie Up. Yes, it's great to experiment. But, being AI-pilled doesn't equate to making the buyer experience better. And, every time you send a "we should be doing this, too" message to the team, you risk distracting them from what actually matters. How they're showing up in buyer interactions. One of the easiest ways to win right now is to outperform in the Sales conversation. Whether that's new logo, renewal, or expansion. Win on the ability to offer an experience that leaves the buyer thinking, "Wow, they came prepared. That was an insightful and useful conversation". Win on reducing their effort to make the case to renew you or buy you. Win on giving a shit about what their business is trying to achieve (vs. just pointing them PowerPoint slides, dashboards, and usage reports and telling a usage story). I'm all for AI that makes the buyer experience better. There are so many ways it can. But, FFS, you don't need to come home from a conference this week and implement every AI tactic you saw someone present on a stage. Buyer experience > everything.

headline: It's NOT you.
text: It's NOT you. Northbeam revealed Meta's performing WORSE Northbeam's data: - CVRs are down as much as 50%. - CTRs hit 12-month highs. - CPMs are up 10-20% since January. - Median CAC climbed 10.3% on 3.3% revenue growth. Why? Auction density keeps climbing. More advertisers, more budget, same finite impressions. And delivery has moved hard toward Reels and broad Advantage+ placements. Those buy cheap, easy clicks from colder people. Higher CTR, lower intent. That combination pulls CVR down even if nothing about your site or offer changed. Here's what I'd work on, in order: 1. Better engagement through better creative → Lead with the problem in the first 2 seconds. → Focus on ads that drive engagement and intrigue to drive CPMs down → Shoot vertical native and create ads that feel like they are edited in platform to reduce instant scrolling → Reply to comments on your top ads so the social proof compounds on the ad itself. 2. CRO → Build a dedicated LP per angle. → If the ad says "for sensitive skin," the LP headline should too. Note that this is not a perfect test, test it dont just push it blind. → Check mobile load time. No.1 site improvement you can make is a faster site imo. 3. AOV through bundling → Default the selection to some sort of bundle → Set the free shipping threshold just above current AOV. → Add one post-purchase upsell that takes a single tap. 4. LTV → Focus on the first 90 days. → Second-purchase offer timed to actual consumption. → Subscription onboarding that cuts cancel rate in month two. It sucks that Meta is performing worse But you have to actively work to find your edge to beat it. Thats the game, passive optimization won’t cut it to grow.

headline: Fairing tracked AI sales at 158 DTC brands
text: Fairing tracked AI sales at 158 DTC brands Results are pretty wild: - Study ran for 104 weeks (Nov-24 to May-26) - Brands spending $10M to $2B a year - Compared UTM against post purchase survey answers 1. Survey vs click gap → Surveys caught 7.5x more AI-influenced orders than click-based attribution → Revenue gap was 10.6x → Click methods captured under 10% of the AI-driven revenue surveys found 2. Growth curve → AI's share of GMV grew 12x year over year → Adobe tracked AI referrals to US retail sites up 14x since Oct 2024 → AI-referred visitors convert 54% better than non-AI traffic, a reversal from a year ago when they converted at half the rate 3. Podcast precedent → Promo codes and vanity URLs catch ~21% of podcast conversions (Podscribe, 66k campaigns) → Pixel-based measurement finds roughly 6x more → ChatGPT is now the no.1 cited discovery source in Fairing's customer base 4. Category spread → High-consideration, high-AOV categories such as mattresses and health devices show the largest AI-driven shares in Fairing's data → In commoditized categories, AI agents default to 1-2 known brands and smaller brands drop out of consideration entirely (Columbia/Yale study) → In housewares, the gap between the most and least AI-attributed brand went from ~2 points to 20+ points in one year 5. Survey fix → Add one question to your post-purchase survey: "Did AI (ChatGPT, Perplexity, etc.) help you find us?" → Wait for 100+ responses and a 30%+ response rate before acting on the split → Then build presence in the sources models cite → And push review velocity - doubling review count gives 17-43% more pricing power when AI agents pick products Is anyone seeing AI mentions climb in their survey responses? headline: I've sold $450M of DTC products
text: I've sold $450M of DTC products I see a NEW arbitrage for premium eCom: AppLovin Ads: → Placements inside mobile games and apps. → The ad takes the full screen. → Rewarded video: the user is locked in for 15-30 seconds to earn extra lives or in-game currency. → Interstitial: a 3-second unskippable window before the Skip button appears. A few years ago I would have laughed at putting a $60 physical product in the middle of someone's mobile game. Going into 2026 and 2027, these networks are performing well for premium eCom brands. (Especially those selling to 40 to 50 year old women.) But you need different creative for AppLovin: Rewarded video (locked in 15-30 seconds) → 0 to 25s: tell a story, show a satisfying demo, entertain them while they wait → 26 to 28s: build tension, this is the riser → 29 to 30s: strongest CTA, timed for the second before they can close it Interstitial (3-second window, then Skip appears) → Don't open on your hook. At second 0 they're annoyed and hunting for the X. → Reverse-engineer it. Seconds 0 to 3 build toward the hook. → The hook lands at second 3, the moment Skip becomes tappable. → This is the opposite of Meta where you're interrupting the scroll and trying to hook for the first 3 seconds. Cheatsheet: - Take your 3 best-performing Meta concepts - Recut the timing around the placement UI - Run rewarded and interstitial as separate tests - Judge the channel on blended MER, in-app attribution is messier than Meta's Anyone else testing AppLovin? headline: HexClad Cookware runs ads at low revenue from Jan to Oct
text: HexClad Cookware runs ads at low revenue from Jan to Oct Makes 50% of their revenue in Nov/Dec How they stay disciplined and why: Who's HexClad? - Premium hybrid cookware (stainless steel + nonstick), sold DTC and in Costco - Gordon Ramsay and Fox invested $100M in 2024, valuing it over $1B - ~$170M revenue in 2022, on track for $350M in 2023, undisclosed after that (541% growth 2021-2024, #775 on Inc. 5000) How they run marketing for the 2-month sale: 1. Two-month sale → ~50% of revenue lands in November and December → 12% of it comes on Black Friday alone → $400 average order value, $699 for the 12-piece set 2. Consideration window → Under 20% of purchases happen inside a 7-day window → 80-85% of buyers say they knew HexClad for months first → Only ~26% of the country is ever "in market" for premium cookware 3. October loss → They run October MER 33% below their year-end target → The 13 days before the sale run about 50% below that → "That's going to allow us to spend into a full funnel" (Connor Rolain, Head of Growth) 4. Black Friday incrementality → ROAS lift peaks over 300% on Nov 12-13, before the sale opens → Black Friday weekend has the lowest lift of the whole period → Jason Panzer, President, left ~$1M of BFCM budget unspent: "It's bottom of funnel now. We did the work all throughout the year." 5. Forecast locked early → Offers, timing and targets set 15 weeks out → 85% of November revenue comes from the sale window → Set expectations to stay the course in October and build demand It's not easy to run marketing like HexClad. You need to have faith in your brand, and forecast incredibly well.

headline: Are your new creatives actually diverse?
text: Are your new creatives actually diverse? How to tell: 1. Download every active ad including ad spend, headline, body, script, on-screen text 2. Transcribe every single ad with timestamps 3. AI tag every ad with format, angle, hook style, creator and core selling point 4. Vectorize every ad so it has a data point on an n-dimensional space 5. Flag the near-duplicates by measuring cosine similarity of >0.95 6. Cluster into concepts by grouping the vectors 7. Measure concentration with Herfindahl index (economists use this to measure market monopolies) If you have too much concentration your account is at risk from fatigue. One idea gets tired, and the whole account goes with it. Summary: - AI tag every ad you run for analysis - Vectorize and measure concentration to go deeper

headline: Did the customer come from Google or Meta?
text: Did the customer come from Google or Meta ? Better way to check: - Pull your post purchase survey responses - Look at answer: "Where did you first hear about us?" - Match each answer to the UTM on that same order. - Create a heatmap grid of where they found you vs UTM codes What you'll see: - Post purchase tends to report awareness channels (TikTok, Meta etc) - UTM tends to report demand capture channels (SEO, Google etc) - Using this you’ll spend less on Google, maybe more on Meta, and more on TikTok. How you use this data: → Use it to know which channels are driving awareness that converts → Push into those channels to grow the brand → Extrapolate the survey across all new customers and calculate cost per new customer per channel. Caveats: → Make sure you have 30%+ response rate before you analyze → Aim for 100+ responses minimum per channel row. And while you're in there, add some more post purchase questions in: "Why did you buy today?" = creative strategy "Anything you almost didn't buy over?" = objection handling "Any issues with the site?" = CRO roadmap "Anything you wish we sold?" = product development Hope this helps

text: Have an in-flight deal that's gone quiet on you? Stop making excuses for your prospect ("I'm sure they're just busy!"). When a deal goes quiet, job #1 is to get to the truth. Here are 3 messages I use to do that (+ when I'd use each one): 1. Unexpected Roadblock I use this when my gut is telling me that something went sideways and the prospect is hesitant to share bad news with me. Fun fact - the more pleasant/nice you are, the harder it often is for a prospect to tell you bad news. People don't like the way they feel about themselves when they tell someone who did their job well, "no". Make it easy for them. 2. The "New Idea" This is my go-to for deals that went quiet a couple quarters ago (works for closed-lost deals, too). It's a way to re-engage them that isn't "want to revisit buying our stuff?". And, it grounds the convo in something happening in their business. Good for when you know your deal isn't attached to anything urgent. 3. "Elephant in the Room" or "Rookie Mistake" I use this when I realize I got happy ears and rushed a deal. I label what I think I goofed and invite the prospect to correct me. This one is especially effective if you didn't help your prospect build the business case. So many deals get stuck here. The best sellers still have deal risk. They're just proactive about addressing the elephant in the room before the prospect does. Try one - and please do let me know if it works for you. I love seeing sellers win. Good luck!

headline: Will your next new ads even work?
text: Will your next new ads even work? How to check: 1. Get all the ads you launched in last 60 days 2. Pull how much each ad spent 3. Categorize into formats / themes 4. Calculate spend per launched ad: Example data for an account: → 511 ads, $2.2M spent → Founder videos: 24 launched, $13k per launch → UGC videos: 91 launched, $7k per launch → Promo statics: 82 launched, $1.6k per launch Promo statics were the second most produced format in the account and near the bottom on dollars per launch. Founder videos were the least produced and top of the list. Two things I'd add if you start running this: 1. Promos need a higher bar → If a promo category isn't beating the account average by a wide margin, it hasn't earned a slot on the production calendar. 2. Bar moves with the account → You're ranking against the account you have right now. The benchmark from someone's blog post doesn't apply, and neither do your January numbers against the June account performance. What are you ranking your creative by right now? Let's discuss.

headline: A moment with my twins reminded me why most GTM outbound fails.
text: A moment with my twins reminded me why most GTM outbound fails. When things get chaotic, the natural reaction is to jump toward whoever is screaming the loudest. The loud scream is just noise. Reacting only to volume means missing the quiet signal of what actually needs fixing. Most revenue teams run their pipeline strategy the exact same way. Everyone buys intent data, CAC is up, and SDR response rates drop. Teams rely on packaged intent platforms where dozens of competitors see the exact same surge score on Tuesday morning. When dozens of competitors see the exact same surge score, every team reaches out to the same buyer with the same message. The buyer gets flooded. Domain reputations burn. Reps waste time chasing phantom interest from a dashboard surge that led nowhere. Packaged intent data is the loud noise. Custom buying signals are the quiet operational indicators that actually turn into pipeline. We closed a $173k deal from a hiring signal no tool tracks because we built our own detection system. Here is how custom signal tracking works: A. Tracking specific tech stack requirements in job descriptions ↳ Look past open job titles ↳ Track the underlying architecture and tools listed inside job requirements ↳ When an account specifies required systems, route directly to outbound B. Champion migrations within 72 hours ↳ Track previous champions and buyers from closed-won accounts when they change companies ↳ Connect early in their tenure before new tooling decisions get locked ↳ Reach out before competitors even register account activity C. RevOps headcount ratio ↳ Track when target accounts shift their operational headcount ratios ↳ Headcount ratio adjustments point to pipeline bottlenecks, reporting friction, or GTM restructuring ↳ Outbound lands when leadership is actively working to solve the problem Fit without signal is a cold list. Signal without fit is noise. If you're not reaching out within 72 hours of a trigger, you're too late. What custom buying signals is your team tracking that off-the-shelf tools miss?

Your closing line, fit without signal is a cold list and signal without fit is noise, is exactly why we built Alsona to weight both into a single lead score rather than ranking on surge alone. It also pulls unstructured intent from across the web instead of one shared database field, so the picture per prospect is not the one every competitor sees on Tuesday morning.

headline: The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real.
text: The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real. Not a sample file. Not the vendor's demo list. Your own interested replies from last week. Somebody who wrote back "yes, I'm interested" has proven their address is a live inbox with a human reading it. So if a validator grades that address catch-all or invalid, you caught it being wrong, and you can count how often. 1. export everyone who gave you a positive reply in the last week or two. that's your answer key. 2. run those through the validator you use today. anything that comes back catch-all or invalid is a miss you can prove. 3. do the same thing on a fresh pull from a provider like Prospeo, then watch the actual bounce rate in production. that's the other half of the picture and it's the half people skip. 4. cost-benefit it for your own volume. I ran ours against Lead Magic, 500 addresses, about a day and a half of positive responses. 14.6% of them graded catch-all, and we throw catch-all in the garbage, so that whole slice would have been deleted off a normal list. Lead Magic validated them. Most validator comparisons are people arguing about brand. This one is just a number you can check, and the answer key is already sitting in your replies folder. I'll drop the short video with the numbers in the comments.

comments.text: Positive replies as the answer key makes total sense. If a known live inbox grades as risky it is a provable miss. Seeing 14.6% marked catch all shows how much pipeline gets tossed for no reason.

The trap when people try this on CRM data: they run the answer key against today's config. Scoring and routing rules get edited after every bad quarter, so the model being tested already knows which deals closed. Does your reply list carry the validator version it was scored against, or just a date?

This is the only validator test that actually means anything your reply folder is a perfect answer key because a human already proved the inbox is live. We started doing the same reverse-check on our own enrichment work and the catch-all miss rate was the biggest surprise: real, replying humans getting graded catch-all and silently deleted. The number that stuck with me is how much "good" pipeline gets thrown away before anyone even sees it.

Using actual positive replies as an answer key is the only reliable way to catch validator blind spots. When we audit outbound data pipelines at MoizWP, relying purely on automated filter categories usually ends up trashing valid leads that happen to sit on catch-all servers. How often do you find your tools flagging verified prospects just because their mail server configuration is overly protective?
what was the highest catch-all rate you noticed when testing the email validator against your interested?

Using your own positive replies as the answer key is the good part here, and it generalises well beyond validators. Anywhere you've got a tool grading something you already know the truth about, you can score the tool instead of arguing about it. The 14.6% is worth sitting with though. That's not a validator accuracy problem so much as a policy problem - binning every catch-all is a rule someone set once, probably sensibly, and it's been quietly eating live inboxes ever since. The tool was only ever doing what it was told.
The day you realize your own replies folder is a better benchmark than any paid comparison, that's about when you stop blindly trusting vendor claims 😂

This same method works on CRM fields, not just email validators. Pull the accounts where a human confirmed industry, size, and use case on an actual call, then check whether your enrichment vendor gets those exact same accounts right. Most people validate enrichment against a spec sheet instead of against reality they've already confirmed. Numbers like your 14.6% only show up once you build a real answer key. What's the next field you'd want to answer key besides email?
This is the test most people skip. From the infra side, unfamiliar signals often get flagged as risky but a real reply is the ultimate proof. No algorithm beats actual human response .
This is how we do it at OrbiSearch - run known bounced emails and known 'good' (successfully delivered) outreach emails through our validator to get a true false positive / false negative rate.

headline: Clay is ruining cold email.
text: Clay is ruining cold email. Take it from someone who spent 4 years sending 300+ outbound emails every single day. Outbound used to be about finding what resonated. You tested a core pain point, measured the response, and refined the message. Today, I watch outbound teams build massive Clay tables to hyper-personalize They scrape every detail they can find on a prospect, generate custom copy for every lead, and hit send. Then the campaign falls flat, and they have no idea why. Start with the offer. Then personalize. Here is the cold outbound testing hierarchy that books me consistent 3.7% positive replies: 1// Test the offer first Find an offer that pulls before writing custom copy. ↳ Keep copy standardized across the test cohort ↳ Zero deep personalization beyond basic account fields ↳ Test distinct value propositions against each other ↳ Run each offer until you establish a clean baseline Target: ~1% baseline positive reply rate on a standardized email. If an audience will not respond to the core offer with standard copy, personalizing the first sentence will not save it. Example: “Would you be interested if I built you a contact list of your past clients who just changed jobs and aren't working with you yet?” 2// Hyper-personalization testing Personalization does work, but it needs to be standardized and tested thoroughly. If you run offer testing against 100+ daily sends, pair it down to 10 per day. This will give you the ability to hyper-customize. ↳ Do a ton of research on the person, a little nugget about them and mention it to them in email, super casual.↳ Then find them on all social platforms possible (Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Facebook)↳ Message them on all those platforms to give you a higher probability of being seen.↳ This takes 10 outreaches per day and 3-4x’s it. ↳ Copy and paste the same message and say “btw I reached out to you via email also” This is how you hit 25% reply rate on a small list. Same impact as 100+ emails per day. 2// Personalization + Offer = Scale ↳ Keep the winning offer and call to action identical ↳ Your manual personalization work will help you ID the 2-3 types of customized messages that work. Wrap them around a specific pain or buying trigger (Clay is great for this part!) Target: scale reply rates up to 3-5%.With buying triggers I see positive replies above 6%. Testing constraints: 1 // Cohorts ↳ 1 industry ↳ 1 buyer committee role ↳ 300 contacts per test cohort ↳ 2 emails per contact 2 // Send limits ↳ Never hit the same contact with more than 1 offer per month ↳ Tag every record with the offer version and cohort outcome This testing system means: - You know exactly which offer generates pipeline - Personalization scales a working message instead of hiding a weak one This is the rigor that outbound teams need.

Your focus on offer-first testing before Clay personalization resonates, how are you incorporating buying signals into cohorts?

Ryan Carlin Offer before personalization is the hierarchy most Clay builds invert. Teams scrape everything, generate custom lines, then wonder why it fell flat: they tested ten variables at once and learned nothing. Standardized copy, one offer pulling, personalization last. 3.7% positive on discipline.

headline: VP of Sales: "We're losing to competitors"
text: VP of Sales: "We're losing to competitors" So I read all 35,000 of their closed lost deals. Not one was tagged competitor. When a revenue number misses, the default suspects are always product, lead gen, or the competition. Then you open the CRM activity logs. On their largest deals, over 18 months: ↳ The median won deal took 13 contact attempts ↳ The median lost deal stopped at 5 ↳ The median disqualified deal stopped at 3 But here's the part that actually matters. With the same deals and size band, the only variable was who owned them: ↳ Top rep: 34% win rate ↳ Team average: 19% ↳ Shared inbound queue: 5% ↳ No owner assigned: 0% The deal didn't decide. The routing did. 55 of those deals were worth $694k combined and were never assigned to anyone. Median contact attempts: zero. They won none of them. And the ones that die don't get closed out. A deal they win closes in 36 days. A deal they lose sits open for 165 days before anyone marks it dead. So reps spend months staring at bloated pipeline, convincing themselves coverage is fine, working deals that died last quarter. Here's the fix: 1 // Fix routing before you fix reps ↳ Kill the shared inbound queue for anything above your ACV threshold & assign it to a human on arrival. ↳ Audit unowned pipeline weekly. Zero is the only acceptable number. ↳ Reassign books held by departed reps within 48 hours, not "eventually." 2 // Enforce persistence thresholds Deals we invested in closed at roughly 10x the rate of deals we didn't. Some of that is that good deals attract effort. Some of it isn't. ↳ Validation rules so opportunities can't be marked closed-lost below a minimum touch count. ↳ Multi-channel, not single-channel bursts. ↳ Track average contact attempts per opportunity by rep, and coach on the gap. 3 // Age out the rot When dead pipeline sits open for 165 days, forecast accuracy is fiction. ↳ Alert the moment a deal exceeds 2x average cycle time. ↳ Stage duration limits: advance it or disqualify it. ↳ Route abandoned accounts back to nurture instead of letting them decay in open pipeline. You don't need more top-of-funnel to hit the number. You need the pipeline you already have to reach a human and a minimum # of touch points per deal. Sales and revenue leaders, what's your minimum touch count before a rep can close something out?

headline: Don't let Meta pick your winning ads
text:
Don't let Meta pick your winning ads

Without doing this:

I recently ran an analysis for a brand with two products.

They were judging their ads on in-platform day-one or 7-day click CPA.

Product A
→ Converted great on day one
→ Tapered off fast after that
→ Lower AOV product
→ Easy decision for the consumer to buy

Product B
→ Looked worse on day-one and 7-day click
→ Longer consideration cycle, higher AOV
→ Ended up the best product after we waited 15+ days
→ Won by even more once we layered in incrementality

Follow Meta's in-platform metrics and we kill Product B. Meta was losing the conversion event proven by incrementality testing, and it is what we have been told to blindly trust.

But there is more to attribution than what Meta reports.

1. Compare 1, 7 and 28-day windows. (Start with in platform then move to incrementality testing)
→ That gap is your purchase velocity. Promos convert inside the 1-day window. Awareness ads show up at 28.
→ A high-AOV ad that looks dead at day 7 could still climbing at day 28.

2. Judge new-customer CPA in your MTA.
→ Triple Whale or Northbeam shows who bought and where they came from first.
→ Meta may miss the ad that opened the consideration cycle. And they report all customers not just new.

3. Give high-AOV ads 30 days before you cut.
→ Days 20-40 is where the repurchases land.
→ Cut at day 7 to look efficient and you never see them.

Day-one CPA tells you which ad converts fastest.
It tells you nothing about which one drives your LTV.

P.S. This isn’t sponsored but Churney has a cool free tool to see how much impact LTV has and if this should be a concern in your account. It isn’t always an issue. Just look up “churney growth predictability test”

headline: How to manage cost/bid cap Meta campaigns
text:
How to manage cost/bid cap Meta campaigns

You need to stay right side of the slope:

You have two dials to achieve high scale and low CPA.
- Moving budget up or down
- Moving bid up or down

If you're under budget:
→ Want better performance? Bid down, budget down.
→ Want more scale? Bid up, budget the same.
→ Want to scale hard? Push both.

The moment you ARE hitting your budget, the bid is how you protect efficiency:
→ Performance just okay? Budget up, bid down.
→ Performance good? Budget up, leave the bid.
→ Performance strong? Budget up, bid up. Let it rip.

headline: I replaced my entire agent setup in about an hour last month, and the only reason it was an hour is a file I made months before I needed it.
text:
I replaced my entire agent setup in about an hour last month, and the only reason it was an hour is a file I made months before I needed it.

Months ago I told Claude Code and Codex to go update a GitHub repo describing who I am and what this business does. Not a README for a codebase. Context. What we sell, how we run campaigns, what our SOPs are, the skills we already had written.

At the time it felt like housekeeping. It turned out to be the thing that made me portable.

When I set up a new agent, the whole onboarding was pointing it at that repo and then one prompt: after you look at my GitHub, make a list of all the tools you are going to need API keys for so I can onboard you.

It came back with Smartlead, OpenAI, Prospeo, Blitz, MillionVerifier, Fathom and the rest of it. So instead of me trying to remember the twenty places my business actually lives, it handed me the checklist and we went down it one at a time.

Then I asked what bots it thought we should have, and it built them.

The lesson I would take from this is not about which tool I moved to. It is that your company context should not live inside any one vendor's memory. The day you want to try something else, everything you know has to be a folder you can point at.

If you have not got that repo, that is the thing to do this week. Ask your coding agent to write down who you are and what you do, and keep it somewhere you own.

comments.text:
The portability point is underrated. We ran into the same thing with our ICP and buyer research files. They used to sit inside whatever tool we were using at the time, and every tool switch meant rebuilding half of it.

One caveat from experience: a context repo is only as good as its last update. Ours drifts within weeks if nobody owns the maintenance, especially around campaign SOPs that change often.

How often do you go back and refresh the repo itself, or does the agent handle that too?

Owning the repo is good hygiene, but it makes you context-sovereign, not vendor-agnostic. The folder is the easy half. What actually makes you portable is a runnable eval suite that pins down how your setup is supposed to behave. Without it you don't know whether the new vendor produces the same output, you only have the feeling that it runs. And that's the trap: a broken setup doesn't announce itself with a bang. The behavior drifts quietly, and you notice it three weeks later in worse output or an edge case that suddenly slips through.

The "your company context shouldn't live inside any one vendor's memory" line is the specific insight most people building on AI haven't internalised yet 🎯 Every agent memory feature is designed to lock you in - the more you invest in teaching it your business, the harder it is to leave. Keeping the context as a repo you own inverts that whole dynamic. Portability becomes the default and vendor switching costs collapse from months to an hour. The "list the API keys you need" prompt is the specific tactical move worth stealing.

The biggest advantage here is making company context portable instead of letting it get trapped inside one AI tool.
Keeping the workflows, SOPs and tools in one repo turns switching agents from a rebuild into a straightforward onboarding process.

Tools come and go, but clarity of purpose endures.
Documenting who you are isn't just about saving time later. It is an act of self-respect. When you truly own your identity and context, you never become hostage to the platforms you borrow. ⚓💡

💯 To be sovereign and vendor-agnostic in any way, you need a place where everything lives which is not vendor specific. And if you optimize this, you have a clearly structured and self explained inventory of your whole company incl. a strictly governed way to keep conceptual hygiene.

headline: IM8 Health launched 10,000 ads since June.
text:
IM8 Health launched 10,000 ads since June.

Isn't that WAY too many???

→ Launched in June, already running 10,000 ads
→ A chunk of the output, in my opinion, is AI slop
→ Their last reported quarter put $22.2M of marketing against $23.3M of gross profit

So why 10,000 ads?

Heres my take:

1. Marketing eats gross profit

→ Q1 revenue $36M, gross profit $23.3M on a 65% margin
→ Selling and marketing came in at $22.2M, so 95% of gross profit went straight back out to acquisition
→ Loss from operations $8.9M, and adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $5.6M from $4.5M a year earlier
→ Net loss reads $23.1M, but $17.8M of that is non-cash marks on digital assets and warrants
→ Revenue grew 6x YoY and the cost base scaled right along with it

2. Orders went backwards

→ Q1 orders came in at 220,000, down from 230,000+ in Q4
→ Revenue climbed 23% QoQ anyway, on $240 new customer AOV and ~79% of new customers subscribing
→ So the growth came out of order value while the customer count fell

3. Someone else funds 70% of CAC

→ General Catalyst's $1B CVF finances up to 70% of IM8's customer acquisition cost
→ It books as a financial liability, repaid out of revenue from those customers
→ The return sits below operating income as interest expense, so it never touches gross margin
→ 100% of the marketing keeps landing in S&M, which is why that line looks so heavy

Payback is ~3.5 months and 70% of the CAC is financed.

Volume is the obvious lever to pull.

But this invites natural failure points
→ Too many low-quality ads
→ Too many ads carrying legal risk
→ Too many near-identical ads splitting the same audience
→ Brand consistency begins to slip

Worth saying those numbers cover January to March. The blitz started in June, so none of it has hit a reported quarter yet. Q2 is guided to $46-48M and May alone did $16.7M.

I'm very curious how the next 12 months pans out...

headline: Knowing a company has 27 people in sales tells you a little bit about their goals as a company.
text:
Knowing a company has 27 people in sales tells you a little bit about their goals as a company. Knowing that 15 of those 27 started in the last six months tells you it's their main focus. 

So we run the same search twice.

First, Clay has a filter called Find Employee Headcount by Criteria. We search for a job function, sales in this case, and that gives us the department as it stands today.

Then we run it again, filtered to only the people who started in the last six months.

The difference between the two numbers is the surge.

One company in the table had 27 in sales with 7 hired recently. Another had 364 with 134 of them hired recently. Deel and Ramp both came back growing their sales teams extremely quickly.

Then the table turns the difference into a percentage, so you can set a bar and stop arguing about whether three hires at a company of 900 counts.

All you enter is the company and the department you care about.

This one is in the free playbook repo in my github for coldoutbound skills. I can link to it in the comments.

headline: For one of our customers we're getting 80 to 100 positive responses a day and I don't touch the account.
text:
For one of our customers we're getting 80 to 100 positive responses a day and I don't touch the account. A Grok bot does four jobs on a cron.

Here's what has to stay true every day or a campaign like this dies.

1. Enough leads in the campaign.

Every day Grok Bot checks how many leads are not started. If it's ever under 100,000 it pulls from our Supabase, which tracks who we emailed in the last 60 days, who we re-reached in the last 30, and what month we last touched them, so nobody gets hit more than once a quarter. Then it fires them at a Clay webhook and the Clay CLI workflow does the cleanup, the enrichment, and the AI content.

2. Volume actually going out.

At noon it checks how many emails went out that day. If something locked up and we're under-sending, it rechecks the campaigns and refills them itself.

3. Daily Deliverability check

It reads our inbox table in Supabase every morning. If a domain was replying at 1.5% and drops to 0.2% day over day, it pulls that domain out, cancels the subscription, and swaps another one in.

4. The Friday inbox destroyer

Every Friday it looks for domains that have sent over 200 emails with under a 0.7% reply rate overall. Those get scheduled for cancellation and pulled out of the campaigns. Then it tells me how many domains we need to buy to replace them. I audit that, make the correction, and put the order in at Hypertide.

The reason it's Grok Bot and not the other agent harnesses is boring. The cron job actually fires. I have set one up in Hermes, then checked in three times wondering why it never ran. 

Codex or Claude schedules can totally do this too but if my computer is off it won't run.

comments.text:
The important part is not just sending more emails, but having the system monitor volume and deliverability without constant manual checks.
Automating the replacement rules also keeps a high volume campaign from quietly degrading over time.

The "boring reason it's Grok - the cron actually fires" line is the specific piece of infrastructure wisdom that separates working agent systems from beautiful ones that don't run 🎯 A scheduler that only works when your laptop is open is functionally broken for any production workflow, and it's the exact detail people skip when they demo their agent stacks. The Friday inbox destroyer plus the daily deliverability check are the real magic though - proactive domain rotation before Google punishes you is what keeps a campaign at 80-100 positives a day instead of collapsing to zero in week six.
The Friday inbox destroyer is smart. Automation that monitors failure and replaces the weak links is where this becomes an actual system.

headline: My twins started preschool this week.
text: My twins started preschool this week. I did not expect to get emotional about it. I knew my wife would be. A few days before, it hit me too. Two and a half years old and out the door. The night before, the school ran a parents only session. Slideshow. Schedule. Policies. Nap procedure. Very organized. Very robotic. I walked out thinking these people have their act together. I was not reassured. Not really. Then came the first day. Parents were still in the room, so I got to watch the teachers work. They were not running the slideshow. They were watching. Reading each kid. Clocking what pulled them in and what shut them down. Adjusting before anything went sideways. An hour in, one of them told me something about my son I had never put into words. That was the moment I got calm. The slideshow was the pitch. The first day was the evidence. I have been hired 9 times to fix a revenue number that was missing target. The candidate who presents well and the operator who steadies the ship are not the same person. Most exec teams find that out in month 6. Here is what actually separates an experienced operator from someone who interviews well: 1 // They do not need domain expertise to move the needle Helpful, not required. Pattern recognition travels. Category knowledge can be bought in 60 days. 2 // They evaluate fast, then decide Short diagnostic window, then calls. Not a 90 day listening tour that produces a deck. 3 // Their early calls are better than 80% right You will know by day 45. Write the decisions down. Score them. 4 // When they do not know, they have the confidence to see it through The tell is not certainty. It is what happens when they are wrong in week 6 and still have it fixed by week 10. Anyone can be good in month one. The job is months 3, 6 and 9. And here is what most exec teams are not seeing. You are watching revenue miss. That part is easy to see, it shows up on a slide. What does not show up is the confidence draining out of the team. Quarter after quarter of leadership not knowing how to fix it, until the org quietly stops believing anyone will. Missed targets are recoverable. Distrust compounds. Keep the wrong leader in the seat, or hire the fourth replacement in three years, and entire departments go into a spiral you cannot hire your way out of. Question for the operators here: What was the earliest real signal you got that a leadership hire was wrong?

headline: Yesterday, I lost a 3000-person January SKO workshop deal.
text:
Yesterday, I lost a 3000-person January SKO workshop deal. Here's exactly what I did to lose it (and how you can lose deals, too). 

First, am I bummed? Of course. It would've been an awesome logo. It had all the markings of a deal that should close. Former client introduced me. On a texting basis with the champion. Champion looped me in with her boss + peers for conversations. She, personally, wanted it to happen. Clear COI against a '27 CEO business objective. 

But, these are exactly the type of deals that used to stay in my pipeline for months. Because I didn't want to hear bad news. So, I didn't make it easy for prospects to give it to me. So, I'd stall until I got desperate for an answer at EOQ.  As a result, I'd leave myself no time to fill my pipeline gap. And, I'd frustrate my manager when my forecast would bottom out 2 days before EOQ. 

One of the great things about my business now is that I HAVE to be better at disqualifying. If I hold a January SKO date, and the customer gives me a no in November, it's unlikely I'll book another one for that day. 

So, here are the two things I did to lose the deal early (that any seller can copy): 

1. In the discovery call, I asked a direct question: "I hope I've earned the right for you to be transparent with me. What, in your opinion, are the most likely reasons your CRO would say no to our idea?". She gave me 2 reasons. 

2. When I didn't hear from her for a couple days, I sent her a text. "Hi! If you hit a sticking point, or heard bad news, you can tell me." Other times, I'll use "Did we hit an unexpected roadblock?". Or, "Did REASON end up happening?". 

The key is that YOU are the one to label the bad news. If you did #1 in discovery, you already know the likely deal threats. Be the one to throw one out in the open, first. If we're wrong, they'll correct us. 

This is especially true if you have good rapport with your prospect. In general, humans don't like the way they feel about themselves when they tell someone they like, "no". Be the one to put the bad news out there, first. 

I got a reply right away that reason #1 was it. "I've been holding out hope that we can keep pushing, but unfortunately.....". 

Of course, it's a bummer to lose a deal. But a GREAT seller has a 30% win rate. That means they lose 7 deals and win 3. 

We can't be afraid to hear bad news. It's part of the job. It's WHEN we hear the bad news that makes the difference. Your time is your most precious commodity.  

Lastly - I sent a note to the leaders I spoke with, thanking them for the opportunity and wishing them a successful SKO. Sales is a long game. How we show grace after a loss matters.

comments.text: I'm clapping for the last parts especially - your embracing of hearing bad news vs. keeping this opp alive, AND sending thank you notes to the team, thereby increasing the odds that they'll call you again. Love love love.

You know I love this...
I'd just add: "I hope I've earned the right for you to be transparent with me." needs to be preceded with actually earning the right for them to be transparent with you. I've heard slimy reps say stuff like that...and I feel like replying, "Uhhh, no." Transparency begets transparency.
Oh, and should I stop going scorched-earth when I lose a deal? Doing the old light-a-bag-of-manure-on-their-front-porch-then-ding-dong-ditch them?

Increasing the velocity of losses are just as important as decreasing the time it takes for the wins. Its actually an interesting Velocity Ratio my past teams measured across our global sales teams. Velocity Ratio = Avg age of Loss / Avg age of Win, where the thinking in a midmarket setting is that on average, a rep should not spend more than 1.5 times longer on a losing deal than they do on a winning deal (=< 1.5) At scale the ratio is an excellent aggregate view of whether teams are deselecting fast enough and reallocating precious time to other funnel opps.

Jen Allen-Knuth The distinction here is everything: you didn’t lose the deal by asking the hard question. You discovered the deal was already lost while there was still time to do something productive with that information. That’s real pipeline discipline.

💯 Sales is a LONG game, transparency up front, allows you to “put your cards on the table” IMO its never a win/loss, no “relationship” is worth burning, because you never know what’s around the corner.
 Keeping your head held high, because you know you did the right thing, not for just you but for the relationship.
Btw “referrals” are still the #1 way to close your deal, you never know who might be one!

Jen, a couple of thoughts. 

* "But a GREAT seller has a 30% win rate. That means they lose 7 deals and win 3". In baseball, if you fail 7 of 10 times, you'll probably get elected to the Hall of Fame.

* "The key is that YOU are the one to label the bad news". The George Costanza model: "It's not you, it's me".

I had a most recent prospect tell me "not interested at this time". With the "at this time", I'll park the opportunity and reconnect sometime down the road. Not the answer I was hoping for now but possibly leading to the answer I am hoping for in the future.
The first question is key… knowing potential risks early at least gives you a fighting chance to solve for them.

Love this story so much. We all lose deals even when we’re doing everything “right” because what we offer isn’t going to be “right” for everyone. And most of the time we can’t know all that until we get into the conversation. Fantastic way you made her feel totally comfortable to tell you the truth early and she, and the leadership, will remember the way you showed up in this circumstance, even though you’re not doing business with them today. Jen Allen-Knuth

The reframe I'd underline: "I HAVE to be better at disqualifying" isn't a mindset shift, it's a structural one — fixed capacity (one SKO slot per date) forces the discipline that willpower alone rarely does on its own. That's the pattern I see with client delivery too: teams that build in real constraints upfront end up making better decisions than the ones just trying to "be more disciplined." The labeling-the-bad-news-first move is genuinely underused, and not just in sales.

This is such an important distinction: bad news isn’t the problem finding it out too late is.
The willingness to ask uncomfortable questions early saves more than just time; it gives you room to make better decisions and keep momentum elsewhere. Great reminder that a healthy pipeline is built on truth, not optimism.

headline: How to know which ads to kill or scale
text:
How to know which ads to kill or scale

1. Take every ad you're running
2. Plot it on a graph
3. Y axis = CPA
4. X axis = Spend (log)
5. Choose your target CPA
6. Define your kill CPA (typically 2-3x tCPA)
7. Draw those lines horizontally

Now you have three types of ads:

Scale = Green
→ CPA below your target line, with spend already behind them
→ Expect about 1% of your ads here. They'll drive 50% of revenue
→ Move budget 20% at a time so you don't trigger relearning

Test = Yellow
→ CPA sits between your target and kill line
→ This is most of your account, usually 65%+ of ads
→ Push more budget and watch where it lands. Drops toward target you scale, climbs past kill you cut

Kill = Red
→ CPA above your kill line with enough spend behind it
→ Enough data to be 90% confident it never hits target
→ Ideally you have zero here. If an ad got this far, you cut too slow

How are you deciding what to cut in your accounts?

I made a FREE tool that lets you upload your Meta CSV data and create this graph yourself.

It runs on your browser, the data is never stored on any server so it’s safe.

comments.text:
This is a much better approach than judging ads purely by ROAS or gut feeling.
The key is separating “not enough data yet” from “this will never work.” A lot of brands kill potential winners too early, while others keep feeding budget into ads that have already proven they won’t hit targets. Data-backed thresholds create a much cleaner scaling process.
Interested. What’s your method for scaling the winning ads? Put them into their own ad set with a minimum spend?
Descent directional framework , but generally high CPA ads needs more spends , so your vertical basline should be diagonal instead

This is such a clean way to visualize spend allocation instead of just eyeballing CPA in a table.
I run mostly Google Ads for e-commerce and dropshipping brands in the US, and the same green, yellow, red logic applies almost exactly to PMax and Search campaigns too. Would love to see a Google Ads version of this tool

The part people usually get wrong with this exact framework: spend threshold alone isn't enough to call "90% confident."

Two ads can hit the same spend but sit at completely different confidence levels if their CPAs came from 3 conversions versus 30. I'd add a minimum conversion count (not just $ spent) before an ad enters the kill zone otherwise you cut ads that just haven't had enough purchase events to stabilize yet, especially post-iOS 14.5 where conversion reporting is already delayed and undercounted.

Spend tells you how much you paid. Conversion volume tells you how much you can trust the CPA you're looking at.

It gets you further than a lot of approaches. I started with this approach and have moved to hold out tests and machine learning. Here’s why:

- CPA assumes perfect tracking data and measures each ad in a vacuum, just like ROAS
- Ad channels work together based on how users consume information, so unless the full customer journey is on one channel, and the sales cycle is somewhere between impulse to 24 hours, the data decays

Instead, measuring all channels as a single system, then isolating to the content level is the best foundation. 

From there you still have to sift out noise and bring in trends. Once you do, you will see the content gaps and missing content that would never have been seen only looking inward at the data inside the business.

Solid approach, much better than judging ads on gut feel alone. Curious how you'd think about layering in business-specific rules on top of the CPA/spend axes, especially for things like ticket variance or longer purchase cycles.
Access

And how do you think this relates to assisted conversions? I ask because many of my campaigns have a high CPA, yet they’re somehow contributing to conversions in other campaigns.

So I always have to look at the blended CAC and the CAC with attribution distributed across them.

The CPA on that graph is only as honest as the CPA feeding it. Most Meta accounts running iOS traffic are undercounting conversions by 20 to 40% because browser pixel drops off, which quietly shoves real winners into your yellow (or even red) zone. Before I kill anything I check the account against server-side CAPI numbers, because I've watched brands cut ads that were actually scale candidates once deduped conversions came back in. Clean signal first, then draw the lines.
An important question. Is it the ad or the campaign. I’ve found it important to normalize ads for where they serve and typical campaign performance. Ad performance alone can be noise.

headline: People tell me cold email doesn't work and then I ask how many emails they sent.
text:
People tell me cold email doesn't work and then I ask how many emails they sent. 300.

Here's the threshold we actually use.

We don't call a campaign successful or unsuccessful until it has sent 1,000 emails.

If it sends 1,000 and gets one positive response, we let it run to 3,000 before we decide anything. Sometimes you just get unlucky, sometimes it is a bad week.

If it sends 1,000 and gets zero positives, we shut it off.

My full belief is that campaigns work quickly or they don't work.

You might have heard Alex Hormozi say he thought he could get outbound implemented in six months and it took a year. Fine, that is true of all of outbound. But that is the booking, the no shows, whether it is the right ICP, the sales process for a cold lead versus a warm one. Everything up to the positive response should show up fast.

So when you hit 1,000 and it is dead, before you rewrite the first line again, go check the two things that are a hard science.

Deliverability. Warmup at 100, the seed list came back clean, reply rate above 1%, the auto responder inboxes coming back over 80%, and whatever campaign you run that always works is still behaving normally.

The list. Have Claude read the whole thing and tell you whether these are actually the people you meant to email, then go look at a hundred of them yourself.

If both of those check out, stop editing the copy. Your problem is the offer, or the framing of it.

headline: I've advised over 100 founders on their content marketing strategy.
text:
I've advised over 100 founders on their content marketing strategy. The first thing I tell them is to write from their lived experience. Here's what I ACTUALLY mean by that:

- Start with a thing that happened, ideally in the last 7 days 

- Say when it happened and who it happened with

- Prioritise being specific and factual over impressive and interesting. e.g. writing about a client call from last Tuesday will build more trust than writing about your best ever year in business

- Share lessons, not advice. Advice is telling people what to do but a lesson is what you found out by doing it. Always write lessons.

- Frame, frame, frame. Show what most people in your market assume, THEN show what you found. 

- If anyone else in your industry could have written it, then it's not worth posting.

- Write it in your own clumsy way. The way you process thought and communicate is unique to you and that is way better than overly polished PC crap.

- If the actual writing part is blocking you from writing, voice note it. Use Wispr Flow to get it all out, then rewrite whatever comes back in your own words.

- Your niche is never too niche. There is an audience for everything. You just need to understand your TAM and reign expectations in accordingly.

None of this requires an impressive result. 

It just requires something to have happened and everyone has something happening to them, especially founders who are juggling business, health, family, relationships etc.

headline: My real benchmark for how smart a model is: does it finish the work.
text:
My real benchmark for how smart a model is: does it finish the work. Here's the loop I run it on every day.

Every day I round up everything that has to get done and all of it goes into ClickUp. Then I open each task and dictate the plan straight into it with Wispr Flow. It is the exact same planning prompt I would write if I were about to sit down and do that task myself.

Then I say one thing. Read all the open tasks in ClickUp, they all have plans inside them, write one gigantic plan with finish conditions on every part of it, hand them out to sub agents, and go do the work. Ask me any clarifying questions you need.

That is my whole day. It is my favorite thing to do with AI and I wish it was easier to show you.

With Opus 4.8 and the models before it, we would get 90% of the way there and the last 10% was a grueling battle every single time.

Fable 5 was the first model that got everything across the line. It listened to the run conditions and the finish conditions the best and it needed the least oversight from me of anything I have run.

Then I looked at my usage. One day of this and Fable had burned 85% of my account and I had to move over to Codex.

I ran the same work on Opus 5 this week. All of it finished, on 8% of my usage.

That is my own run on my own tasks, so take it as one data point and not a benchmark.

The reason the plan lives in ClickUp and not in a chat window is that the task is already where I write down what done looks like. The model gets the goal and the finish condition in the same place every time, and I never re-explain it.

comments.text: There is a deeper implication here for how teams run AI on real work. When the criteria live where the work happens, quality stops depending on whoever remembers to ask the right questions. I see the same pattern in go-to-market research. The systems that hold up are the ones where the definition of done is baked into the workflow itself, and anyone can pick up a task without losing context.

The "plan lives in ClickUp not in the chat window" bit is the specific workflow choice most people miss when they're setting this up 🎯 Every re-explanation of what "done" looks like is a place the model can drift, and putting the finish condition in the same system the task lives in removes that gap entirely. The 85% vs 8% usage comparison between Fable 5 and Opus 5 is the interesting data point - not the benchmark, but the fact that model choice at this level of orchestration is now a real cost decision, not just a quality one.
Finish conditions are probably doing a lot of the heavy lifting here. AI gets much more useful when “done” is clearly defined instead of leaving the model to decide when to stop.
The finish condition is what makes this approach practical. Giving the model the goal, plan, and definition of done in the task itself reduces the need for constant back and forth.
Putting the finish conditions right in the task itself really saves so much back-and-forth. It’s so much easier to hand things off that way......no one’s guessing what success looks like.

headline: Prospects are bored out of their minds with our outbound messages.
text:
Prospects are bored out of their minds with our outbound messages. 

We're living through one of the craziest periods of change we've seen in a long time. 

And, we're out here writing "We help companies like you streamline XYZ...", expecting that our prospects will respond with, "WOW, YOU DO??? LFG!!!!!!! IS THERE AI INVOLVED?? OMG, THERE IS???"

Every executive is under pressure to gain a competitive edge. 

And, every great vendor is sitting on a wealth of ideas for how they can do that. 

But, we're so eager to talk about our "leading AI platforms", that we hide that ball. 

It's BORING. We're BORING. 

Want prospects to get excited about your message? 

Put your product on the back burner for a minute.

Go learn like your buyer learns. Consume your company's SME content. Read "State of" reports. Go to industry conference pages and study the list of topics + who is speaking. Go to industry webinars. Join Slack communities and look for the "how are you approaching XYZ..." questions". Listen to Gong calls with smart customers. Follow the most forward-thinking execs and voices in your target persona and consume their content. 

This will give you a bank of stories + ideas. Even if it means *gasp* sharing a few ideas outside of your solution domain, too. 

In every one of my clients, there is at least 1 seller doing this well. And, they're killing it. Everyone else wants to know how they do it. Until they realize how much effort it requires. It's much easier to ask, "What's a good cold email template I can use?". 

It's not an easy time to sell. But, that's the point. The hard work works BECAUSE it's hard. 

Now is the time to get so curious about what fundamental questions your target persona is trying to answer. 

Send messages with "Had an idea re:.." instead of "I'd love to show you a demo of our..".

Do this well and I promise you it'll open the door to a convo about your stuff.

xoxoxoxo

headline: I ran GTM at a $23M SaaS
text: I ran GTM at a $23M SaaS We grew 43% when we measured sales and marketing against the same metric: Pipeline Velocity = (Qualified Opps × Win % × ACV) / Sales Cycle Length Constraint ownership: ↳ Qualified opp volume drops → Marketing owns the 7-day fix ↳ Win rate drops → Sales diagnosis ↳ ACV drops → Check discounting first. Discounts up = Sales. Discounts flat, smaller logos = Marketing is sourcing the wrong segment ↳ Cycle length stretches → Sales analyzes stage by stage (pre-meeting = Marketing) ↳ Everything drops at once → ICP mismatch (joint war room) Here is the exact RevOps architecture we used to scale from $16M to $23M ARR in 16 months: 1 // The CRM Object Model: Fit + Signal Tiers Most CRMs are graveyards of unworked leads with no account context. We restructured the account object into 3 operational tiers and rolled every lead up to it: ↳ Tier 1 (Active Demand): Full ICP fit + 2 verified buying triggers in last 30 days. Routed directly to SDRs who reached out within 1hr ↳ Tier 2 (Fit, Low Signal): enrolled in stage-matched ABM air cover and nurture tracks ↳ Tier 3 (Signal, Poor Fit). auto-DQ to preserve SDR capacity We required two fields on every target account: ↳ Committee Coverage Score: number of buying roles mapped out of the total for that segment. No deal moves past discovery with fewer than 3, and a single-threaded deal in Stage 3+ triggers a manager review. ↳ Trigger Timestamp (hiring surges, new tech install, leadership change) 2 // Routing & Speed-to-Lead Automation ↳ Inbound speed-to-lead: in our data, leads touched in <1 hour converted 2.8x better than leads touched after 24 hours ↳ Outbound rules: SDRs never reach out off cold lists. They sequence only when the account is Tier 1 and trigger is under 72 hours old ↳ Pre-call enrichment: Clay auto-populates the likely economic buyer and technical evaluator onto the account ahead of disco call, so the AE knows who to multi-thread toward. 3 // The Monday 9am Operating Cadence Every Monday morning, leadership received 3 dashboards: Report 1: GTM Efficiency ↳ Magic Number: annualized net new ARR ÷ prior-quarter S&M spend. ↳ CAC Payback by segment: Mid-Market came down from 15 to 11 months. ↳ LTV:CAC by channel: scale at 3:1, breakeven is 2:1, kill anything that stays under 2:1 for two quarters. Report 2: Funnel Health ↳ Pipeline coverage by segment: 3x SMB, 4x Enterprise, reviewed against next-quarter quota↳ Deal aging: automated alert when an opportunity exceeds 2x average stage duration↳ Concentration risk: flag when 1 deal represents >25% of total pipeline Report 3: Forecast Accuracy ↳ MAPE score by segment ↳ Bias detection: identifies consistent sandbagging vs optimistic forecasting ↳ Slippage risk: deals with no champion touch in the last 14 days. This meant leadership walked into Monday knowing the 2-3 pipeline constraints to solve asap 1 formula, simple system architecture and 3 reports will steady the ship through Q4. headline: Most new in role lists are wrong in the same way, and the fix is one column.

headline: Until 2021, I was firmly on the gold line here.

- choices i make in my personal life

Sharing my thinking on the internet under my own name.

→ Incremental conversions ÷ platform-reported conversions = your incrementality rate.
→ Platform ROAS × that rate = true ROAS.
→ One brand reported 5x on retargeting. Revenue stayed flat with it off. 12.5% of those conversions were incremental, so true ROAS was 0.63x.
→ The number finance gets: discount platform retargeting revenue by 87.5%.

2. Geo holdout

→ Spend heavily in a few selected regions, hold the rest flat, measure the lift.
→ Test region revenue growth minus control region growth = your lift.
→ Extra spend in the test region ÷ incremental conversions = incremental CPA.
→ Incremental CPA ÷ platform-reported CPA = the adjustment factor for that channel.
→ Cross-check that lift against your post-purchase survey for the same window.
→ Scale only where that incremental CPA clears your break-even CPA.

3. Account-wide lift test

→ From the day a high-scaling top-of-funnel ad launches, ignore net-new launches and track aggregate ROAS of the ads already running.
→ Baseline that cohort's ROAS for the 30 days before launch. It should decline softly.
→ Cohort ROAS during the scaling window minus that baseline trend = the halo the ad is generating.
→ Example, one TOF ad: ROAS on everything else rose 45% while it ran, down 24% when paused.

4. MER and contribution margin

→ Lead the weekly report with contribution margin split across your highest value ads, sat next to revenue.
→ MER = total revenue ÷ total marketing spend.
→ Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin. At 60% margin that is 1.67x.
→ Report every channel against that line.

5. Survey vs last click

→ Compare your post purchase survey responses to last click UTM.
→ Survey share of a channel ÷ last click share of that channel = your adjustment multiplier.
→ If the survey shows 1.5x what Meta reports, Meta's number gets multiplied by 1.5.
→ Hand over one multiplier per channel, with the response count it came from.

6. Conversion window

→ Click attribution overvalues lower funnel by up to 250%. (Haus has shared great data here)
→ Top of funnel drives 13x more incremental acquisitions than bottom of funnel.
→ Days 20-40 is the biggest repurchase window, so a 1 day view window grades your best ads before they have done anything.
→ Same ad on a 7 day click window ÷ that ad on a 1 day view window = what your reporting window is costing top of funnel.
→ Apply a window multiplier to every top of funnel ad

headline: Here's how I found 73 positive replies we had been throwing in the garbage.
text:
Here's how I found 73 positive replies we had been throwing in the garbage.

Jesse Ouellette at LeadMagic kept telling me to try his email validation. He said he knows catch-all emails better than anybody else. I said sure man, I'm sure you do.

So I ran a test on emails I could not argue with.

I pulled 500 addresses that had just sent us a positive response at the agency. About a day and a half of interested replies. Every one of those is a real inbox with a real person behind it, because the person already wrote back to us.

I ran them through the validation we already use. 14.6% graded catch-all.

We throw catch-all in the garbage. We don't send to it. So on a normal list, that 14.6% gets deleted before anybody ever mails it.

Lead Magic validated those same addresses. It did not miss them.

That is 73 positive replies we would never have gotten, on a day and a half of responses.

But catch-all is the slice of every list that almost nobody sends to, and Jesse has put a lot of work into resolving it specifically. That is a real chunk of reachable people sitting in a folder you already paid for.

Run the same test on your own interested replies before you take my word for any of it. Pricing is great and the API is fast.

headline: Imagine if every time you sent a cold email, your prospect had the option to click a button inside of Gmail or Outlook that graded your email A-F.
text:
Imagine if every time you sent a cold email, your prospect had the option to click a button inside of Gmail or Outlook that graded your email A-F. And, that grade went into a public-facing Sales Experience score (like a Yelp score) towards both your employer and you, personally. 

Same for cold calls. Apple and Samsung added a button.

Same for discovery calls and demos. Zoom, Microsoft, and Google Meet added a button. 

Your score stayed with you throughout your entire career. Your employer's score was an average of every seller's score on the team. 

Sales has spent the last 20 years finding ways to use technology to make the job easier for us and the experience worse for our buyers. 

Ex: AI personalization-at-scale. 

Personalization worked because it required intentional thought. Now, it simply requires a bot scraping LinkedIn posts. 

It's why today's AI personalization often sounds like, "Saw you went to a KISS concert in 2018. Anyhow, we're the leading provider of IT and engineering talent...". 

Do you think the tables will eventually turn?

(Personally, I hope it does.)

comments.text:
OMG - love it... like an Uber score. 
Imagine how we might act differently if this existed. 
The score would shoot up before you picked up the phone, or opened the email... So if you see a score of less than four out of five, for example, you can decide not to pick up the email or pick up the call. Or worse (or better?) you can set an auto default that anyone who calls or emails you with a score below X you just put to spam or ignore.

I really do think it’d be legit to create “baseball cards” for sellers as a standard. Where you see career stats / buyer ratings over time. 

Maybe a future part of BuyerExperience’s roadmap??

Ironically, i get emails that are TOO personalized which makes it obvious it was from scraping info from my profile and site.  My recent favorite was two emails in a row from "humans" (i looked them up and they don't exist, but had real first and last names) that literally regurgitated the summary of my book back to me from what it scraped from the site and then asked for a call.  No one talks like that - it's weird.  I'll admit I use AI at times for scaled outreach, but I do it very sparingly and try really hard to just write a message that is in my voice and targeted to the specific ICP it is intended for to hopefully provide something of value.  I accept in sales we need to put ourselves out there, but we can do better.

So using implicit data and explicit (ratings) data has been used quite extensively in AI for more than 2 decades. What smart companies do is balance the explicit with the implicit to come up with hopefully accurate predictions. Our elections use small samples of explicit Q/A to gauge early results polling. That is how we rate support calls for IT/Customer Support Service help desks. Ecommerce sites monitor your explicit activity and ask you rate experience all that data is consumed as part of the training data for the algorithms. LinkedIn (likes). It has not gotten better because it is hard, preferences are not static, humans are fickle, humans don't tell the truth, models not great, algorithms not dynamic enough, data incomplete, and so on.

I’m all for holding sellers accountable for the buyer experience, but I’d be careful making buyer ratings the scorecard. Great salespeople ask hard questions, push back and create urgency. That won’t always earn them five stars, but it can still create a great sales experience.

This is a great thought experiment because it exposes who the tools are actually built for. Same pattern shows up in operations — automation gets adopted because it makes the internal process faster, not because it makes the client experience better, and those two goals quietly drift apart if nobody's measuring the second one. A visible score would force accountability that volume metrics never will.

I think the tables already are turning a bit, the more AI makes it possible to send "personalized" outreach at zero effort, the less personalization itself means anything and the bar moves back to judgment: was this actually the right person, was there a real reason to reach out now, and did the message earn the interruption? that’s probably a healthier direction for sales anyway, i'm on board.

We deal with this constantly on the outreach side. A researched detail and real personalization aren't the same thing. If the fact doesn't actually connect to the pitch that follows, the prospect can tell nobody read what they found, they just scraped it. I don't think the tables turn until buyers get faster at spotting that gap than sellers get at faking it.

The part of this score that would sting most is not the pitch, it is what happens after the deal is signed. Buyers remember the rep who said I will check on that and get back to you Friday and then went quiet for three weeks more than they remember a slightly generic opener. A public score on kept promises during onboarding would do more to fix trust than grading the cold email ever could. Would you weight the post sale behavior the same as the pre sale pitch, or heavier?

Jen Allen-Knuth The button sort of exists already, it's just invisible. Mark-as-spam is the F grade, and it follows the domain, not the rep. Deliverability is the Yelp score nobody checks until the whole team's emails quietly stop landing. The scoring turned years ago, we just don't see our grade.

headline: Everyone's decided content is finished because AI can write it.
text:

Write about the last time you did something.

None of this stuff is publicly available. It's all in your head.

headline: How to still run broad Meta targeting
text:
How to still run broad Meta targeting

But still target your best audiences:

- We still want to run broad targeting without shrinking auction pool
- We want to let Meta find the best customer, but still want to guide it

Here's how to do it: 

1. Open value rules

→ Ad set level > Optimization & Delivery > Value rules > Create rule.

2. Pick the segment

→ Age, gender, location, or a custom audience.

3. Set the multiplier

→ Segment running a 20% higher CAC? Set 0.8.
→ Segment with 2x the repeat purchase rate? Set 1.2.
→ Meta keeps bidding on them with a higher or lower weighting

4. Audience Network

→ The one hard exclusion worth making. Ad set > Placements > Manual, uncheck Audience Network.
→ It takes 10-20% of spend and returns 40% CTRs with near-zero CVR.

Note: if you don't know your best demos: 

→ Age and gender: Breakdown > By Delivery > Age, then Gender. 
→ Country and region: Breakdown > By Delivery > Country, then Region. 
→ Placement: Breakdown > By Delivery > Placement.
→ Platform and device: Breakdown > By Delivery > Platform & Device. 
→ Time of day: Breakdown > By Time > Time of Day (Viewer's). 

Cheatsheet:

- Bid down before you exclude. Every exclusion raises your CPMs.
- 0.8 on a segment costing 20% more. 1.2 on your best cohort.
- Audience Network is the one hard cut worth making.
- Pull the matching breakdown for every setting you choose. Monthly.

Anyone running value rules?

comments.text: Broad works so much better when you give Meta the right signals instead of trying to control every little thing. The “bid down before you exclude” part is key.

Interesting approach to guiding broad targeting without unnecessarily shrinking the auction pool. The key seems to be using actual conversion and customer value data to adjust weighting rather than relying on assumptions. Curious how consistently value rules outperform simple exclusions in your tests.

Solid framework. One nuance on Audience Network — the hard exclusion makes sense for conversion/catalog campaigns, but for awareness or app-install objectives it's often still worth keeping. Lower CPMs, different job to do. Worth splitting the "should I exclude AN" decision by objective, not applying it account-wide.

Good breakdown. One thing I have seen with value rules on broad targeting is that they only pay off if creative supply matches the segments you are weighting up. If you push 1.2 on a repeat purchase cohort but every ad running is a cold acquisition hook, Meta still struggles to serve that segment efficiently. Worth splitting creative testing by the same segments you use in the value rules, not just the bid weighting.
Without enough conversions per segment, those multipliers look smart on paper and barely move who actually gets reached.
Value rules are so underused it's wild. Most people either go full manual exclusion and strangle the auction, or leave it fully broad and just hope for the best.
The Audience Network cut is the one everyone sleeps on. 40% CTRs with near-zero CVR is exactly the trap. Value rules on top of that is a clean way to guide broad without killing the pool.
Just starting to test into it with my clients. Thanks for this framework! Will be an interesting next few months trying to pull on the right levers.
Just make sure you have an unbelievable conversion event that correlates with revenue in the future. Broad targeting is the best but it needs a good signal.
