headline: What Meta ads bid strategy is best?
text:
What Meta ads bid strategy is best?

Full breakdown:

1. Highest Volume

→ You choose the budget. Meta spends it all.
→ Your CPA will vary to ensure the full spend.

2. Cost per Result Goal

→ You lock in a cost target.
→ A cost target rejects expensive conversions. And if cheap conversions aren't possible then you'll spend less money.
→ Set the target below your recent CPA and Meta stops bidding.
→ Meta notes: "Adherence to cost per result goal limits is not guaranteed."
→ Set it 10-20% above recent CPA and control budget by moving the cost target up and down.

3. Bid Cap

→ You lock the bid in every auction.
→ Your spend varies to whatever it takes to meet that bid.
→ This is useful when you know your exact break-even to the dollar and you're fine spending varying budgets as a result.
→ Meta notes it "does not control for the CPA that you see in reporting." You control the bid. The reported CPA is whatever the auctions produce.

How I use bidding strategies

- Highest Volume until I have a baseline CPA.
- Test a cost target after that, to steer budget and bids in and out of the right ads. Compare on performance.
- Almost never bid cap.

comments.text:
I like the “Highest Volume until I have a baseline CPA” approach. It’s tempting to start optimising before you actually have enough data to know what good looks like. That's also how I think about finding winning ad creatives that brands can then produce at scale. 

I also like your visual. Makes the difference in spend and cost pretty clear too

IMO there's very good reason to run these in parallel long-term (at least when ad spend is over $1M/month).

Similar to how different creatives reach different audiences, different bid strategies can reach different audiences.
Spot on Curtis. The baseline CPA first is the step most people skip, jumping to a cost target with no reference just handcuffs Meta before it learns anything.

One additional callout in favor of highest volume is creative testing. With cost targets and bid caps, you limit how quickly Meta can find the right audience for new creative. You limit your learning velocity. You limit the depth of learning you might get out of a creative by limiting the audience it could serve to. 

Sometimes the best ad is the one that is 2x your CAC target, but teaches you something that you use to create the winner in your account. 

Highest volume = best learning

The missing decision criterion is incrementality. A cost goal can improve reported CPA by concentrating delivery on conversions that are cheaper to capture and attribute, without necessarily improving marginal revenue or profit. At meaningful scale, I'd use the platform read to manage execution, but settle the bid-strategy decision with a geo holdout or conversion-lift test; the Gordon/Zettelmeyer Facebook experiments are a useful reminder that observational purchase-lift estimates were off by 3x or more in half of the studies.

The “you can hold cost steady or spend steady, not both” point is a really useful way to think about Meta bidding. I also like the practical approach of using Highest Volume to establish a baseline before testing Cost per Result Goal. Makes the strategy much easier to apply rather than just theoretical.

One thing worth adding to the cost target piece that "recent CPA" baseline is only as reliable as your EMQ.
 
If EMQ is swinging between 4 and 7 (which happens more than people admit, usually from inconsistent fbp/fbc passthrough), your "baseline CPA" isn't a stable number, it's noise from Meta scoring the same conversions differently week to week. Set a cost target off a noisy baseline and you're not steering budget, you're chasing a number that moves for reasons that have nothing to do with bid strategy.
 
Worth checking EMQ stability before locking any cost target, not after.
So highest volume spent a third more and achieved a lower CPA? Any thesis on why Curtis Howland ? And given that why would you ever move to cost per result goal?
Curtis Howland Exactly - start wide to learn the real per-customer cost, then test a cost target to steer spend and bids; lock a fixed bid only when profitability is an exact dollar figure.
Rejecting expensive conversions can starve learning when volume collapses under a tight cost target.

headline: Running influencers/podcasts for your DTC?
text:
Running influencers/podcasts for your DTC?

How to attribute the right way:

We audited podcast and creator spend for a brand
- On last-touch, the numbers looked awful.
- CPA hit over 10x target on some placements based on coupon codes.
- Half of the creators’ placements drove nothing tracked in the affiliate portal.
- A ROAS-brained media-buyer would mark this as a failed channel

Here's why those tracking models are wrong for this:
- Users listen to podcasts driving, or at the gym.
- But then they search your brand on Google three days later and buy.
- Last-touch credits that sale to organic search. The podcast gets nothing.
- Promo codes and vanity URLs catch about 21% of podcast conversions (Podscribe, 66k campaigns).

Instead:
- Run post purchase surveys PPS and ask "where did you hear about us"
- Measure responses and calculate PPS CAC
- On this audit, PPS CAC came in at $25
- That was very strong (target around $28 in this case).

Takeaway = be very careful using last touch CAC for top funnel marketing activities

comments.text: This is why I’ve never liked judging every channel with the same attribution model. A podcast and a branded search ad are doing completely different jobs in the journey.

headline: There are two reasons why marketers are the first to get laid off:
text: There are two reasons why marketers are the first to get laid off: 1. they struggle to tie their activities to revenue. 2. activities are difficult to measure Sales is a function of the number of activities performed. Marketing is a disconnected maze of engagement that will never be perfect to track. Which means your influence as a marketer is always in question. Any fractional role I take - this is usually the first system I set. It tells a connected story from top of funnel engagement all the way to revenue, and it records the activities along the way. For B2B: 1. Produce expert content and post it on LinkedIn. You’ll learn quickly what your audience connects with and what is on the bleeding edge in your industry. 2. Run ads against your best performing posts 3. As accounts engage, record their engagement signal in a Database (I use Supabase) 4. When a signal is captured, the account gets matched against your ICP qualifications 5. If it passes, enrich the account with every contact at the company. 6. Then enrich for any buying triggers (funding announcements, new hires, news etc.) 7. Run this data up to the account record in your CRM Most would run outbound off the warm account. But we don’t. An SDR only receives the lead when: A signal is captured AND a Buying Trigger is present. This is how we help our clients 3x reply rates and hit 55% close rates. Marketers that can prove a lead source, tie it directly to revenue stays, and work hand in hand with Sales are the types that stay in-seat for 15+ years. Go do it.

headline: I'm working with a $55m arr tech company
text: I'm working with a $55m arr tech company Found 2 reasons why their outbound wasn't converting. Here's the fix: 1. Personalization. I get this is controversial and against every 2026 playbook - show me you know me works, but it needs to be done with the simplest and shortest copy possible. For complex b2b, this wasn't possible. We removed all personalization and went straight to the offer. Template: "If we could [Improvement] your [product] - would you be interested? Examples: "If we could cut your churn in half without adding CS headcount in 45 days" "If we could cut your onboarding time in half" "If we could 3x your expansion revenue in 60 days" "If we could build you 3 ai agents for free" 2. Buying triggers were receiving cold email (only). Just because a company is ready to buy, doesn't mean you'll be able to reach them by email. It also doesn't mean their are ready for a conversation. Let's say you're product is a CS chat bot that drives expansion revenue. And your Buying Trigger is found that your target company is Hiring a first VP of Customer Success. You have a 60 day window to convince the VP to replace their current tool with yours. If you think an email drip is all you need to get the meeting - your SOL 98% of the time. Here's the real playbook: 1. Buying trigger is identified 2. Auto-enrich the account with current tech stack - find the chatbot they are currently using ( Sumble is great for this) 3. Run competitor displacement ads for the first 90 days the VP hired 4. Sequence the email drip 5. On day 45, create a pattern interrupt. For this deal (yes it's real), we gifted a coffee cart outside their office - "Your chatbot can't do this either." The CCO and Head of sales were serving up the coffee. 6. Find the champion (never decision maker) and run an incentive program Playbook: signal id > enrich > air cover ads > pattern interrupt > champion incentive This is how you win when you're not the market leader. headline: Here's a creative outbound tactic I learned from an AE this week.
text:
Here's a creative outbound tactic I learned from an AE this week. Most importantly, he's booking meetings with VP+ prospects with it. 

As context, I've spent the last 2 days in London, running outbound & discovery workshops with a Sales team at Bloomberg Industry Group. 

Yassine Dessouki is one of the sellers. He was a former professional DJ, now selling into Tax leaders. Backgrounds like his always interest me. Creatives tend to approach the job differently, in the best of ways. 

Yassine sells into Heads of Tax at Enterprise companies. When you picture a VP, Tax - what comes to mind? A buttoned-up, stiff, corporate person in a suit? Surely, no sense of humor, right? 

Yassine understands that an executive is not defined by their title. Most Tax leaders don't go home and spend their evenings creating more Excel spreadsheets for fun. They have hobbies, they have favorite TV shows, they have a sense of humor - just like the rest of us. 

So, here's a breakdown of exactly what he's doing (he sends these via LinkedIn DMs):

1. He learns about the company. What's their tagline? What do they do? What does their product do? 
2. He comes up with a clever tagline that shows he has an understanding of his clients' business. 
3. He uses AI to create a meme, using their image, in a scene that ties the two companies together. 

Two Examples: 

Maybelline: Their tagline is "because you're worth it". His meme? "Because your tax strategy is worth it". Image of his prospect in what looks like a makeup ad, with tax laws on the makeup labels. 

Lego: "Building your tax strategy together",  with an image of his prospect assembling Legos with different tax law names on each Lego. 

He writes one line of text to accompany it. No long diatribe. The image tells his story. 

Yassine gave me permission to share this. 

Because he knows that strategies like this only work if the seller puts thought into understanding the prospect's business and finding a clever way to make the connection. And, most sellers won't take the time to do that. Because it doesn't scale. 

And, that's exactly why it works. 

As I always say, nothing always works and nothing never works. Especially when it comes to outbound. But, I love seeing sellers like Yassine get creative.

comments.text: If someone sent a meme of me in Chanel, I’m definitely buying whatever they’re selling. Smart man 👏🏼

I think that today only brand familiarity, creativity, and/or humor help to get a reply. Personalization the way we know it became a commodity, like "I've seen you....". Standing out in outreach is not optional anymore.

The "doesn't scale so it works" line is the whole game with senior outbound. I've tested one-off personalized visuals into VP-level prospects and the hit rate wasn't about the meme itself, it was that the prospect could tell a human actually looked at their site for ten minutes instead of running a template.

This is right up my alley and I love it! I too have been seeing success with tying an experience or something creative to a genuine business problem. For the first to work, you have to do a *lot* of homework and nail your research to get it right.

I listened to you on 30 Minutes to President’s Club yesterday and got so much value from the conversation that I had to follow you here!

What I love about this example is that Yassine hasn’t tried to fit himself into a conventional sales persona. He’s taken his natural creativity and turned it into a real advantage, using it alongside thoughtful research to create genuine connections and start conversations. Such a great reminder that the qualities that make someone different can also be what makes them exceptional in sales.
Thinking outside the box! Curious though - do any of the prospects find it weird seeing their AI selves in a meme outreach?
I love this. “Because it doesn’t scale” might actually be my favorite part. The stuff that clearly took a little thought is so much harder to ignore.

Also, Stu Heinecke should know about this! This reminds me a bit of his work creating custom cartoons for his targets. While all of us aren't award winning artists, there are still so many things we could be doing to show people that we give a hoot and did our research.

What strikes me is the operational insight hiding inside this — Yassine's approach only works because he's willing to spend time on something that doesn't scale, at exactly the stage when most sales orgs are optimizing for volume. That's the same tension I see with founders building processes: the instinct to systematize everything can quietly kill the judgment and creativity that actually made something work in the first place. Some things are worth keeping manual and personal, even as everything else gets automated.

That tagline mashup is the part doing the work, the meme is just the delivery, because a Head of Tax can tell in one glance whether you actually read their business or ran their logo through a tool. You flagged the DJ background as the reason he thinks this way, so I'm curious whether that same creative instinct shows up once he's in the room, or if it's mostly the opening where it pays off.

headline: When you're marketing and sales teams don't communicate
text:
When you're marketing and sales teams don't communicate

Run them off a named account list. Here's the full signal-based playbook:

1. Marketing & Sales leadership decide on a single ICP (e.g. "Software & IT / USA / 500-1k employees)

2. Marketing responsibilities:
↳ Break down the Buyer Committee roles
↳ Run offer testing. Cold Email and a new offer to every 300 contacts inside each buyer committee role.
↳ Find 1 message per persona that hits above a 1% positive reply rate
↳ This is the core of your messaging docs

3. SDR/BDR Responsibilities
↳ Find accounts that match the ICP (use: DiscoLike, Ocean.io, AI Ark & Clay)
↳ Find prospects that match the buyer committee roles. Enrich Champion, Decision Maker, Influencer at minimum.

Collab point: Marketing brings the messaging, sales brings the accounts and contacts & outreach begins on offer testing.

Marketing simultaneously runs ads against the account & contact lists.

4. RevOps tracks 3 signal types:
a. Signal 1: marketing ad engagement & clicks
b. Signal 2: email negative and positive responses
c. Signal 3: buying triggers. Funding events, return to office, job posting data, new hires & champions.

↳ Revops tracks these signals in a database. It routes all signals to the account record in your crm.

5. Signal scoring in the CRM
↳ Each signal type has a point score and decay.
↳ Points total against awareness stages e.g.:

0 points: Identified
1-25 points: Aware
26-75: Interested
76-120: Considering
121+: [sales pipeline; hard requirement: meeting booked]

Benefits:
↳ Sales team knows who to call right now
↳ Marketing has clear responsibility tied to real pipeline outcomes.
↳ Highly prescriptive: clear gates on what needs to be achieved to move accounts.
↳ Clear, reportable record of account progression through awareness stages

Outcomes (Avg. Exit Engine client results):
↳ Sales cycle time cut by 30%
↳ Deal sizes increase by 22%
↳ Marketing sourced pipeline (avg): 38% yoy increase
↳ Close rates increase 68%

↠ what signals are you tracking?

headline: I've audited 200+ ABM programs
text:
I've audited 200+ ABM programs

The biggest predictor of ABM success isn't your ICP, messaging, or your team. 

It’s a financial issue

The first question I always ask:

“Walk me through the math. What are we actually buying here?”

Maybe 5 had a defensible answer.

The ABM programs that get renewed are decided before launch, not after.

Here’s how to set it up correctly:

STEP 1 // BUILD YOUR COST MODEL

Total ABM investment breaks into 3 buckets:

A. Media spend
↳ LinkedIn, CTV, programmatic, direct mail
↳ Budget $150-300 per target account per month for air cover
↳ 100 accounts = $15K-$30K/month minimum

B. Tech stack
↳ Intent data, ABM platform, enrichment tools
↳ Annualize and divide by # of programs

C. People cost
↳ % of SDR, marketing, ops time dedicated to ABM
↳ Burdened salary × time allocation

Add all three = Total Program Cost

STEP 2 // MODEL YOUR EXPECTED PIPELINE

Formula:
Target Accounts × Expected Engagement Rate × Meeting Conversion × Opp Conversion × Avg Deal Size = Expected Pipeline

Example with real math:
↳ 100 accounts
↳ 25% engagement rate (25 engaged accounts)
↳ 40% meeting conversion (10 meetings)
↳ 70% opp conversion (7 opportunities)
↳ $75K avg deal size
= $525K in pipeline

STEP 3 // CALCULATE PROGRAM ROI

Pipeline ROI = Expected Pipeline / Total Program Cost

If your program costs $50K and generates $525K in pipeline:
↳ Pipeline ROI = 10.5x

But leadership cares about closed revenue, not pipeline.

Revenue ROI = (Expected Pipeline × Historical Close Rate) / Total Program Cost

↳ $525K × 30% close rate = $157.5K expected revenue
↳ $157.5K / $50K = 3.15x revenue ROI

STEP 4 // BUILD THE SENSITIVITY TABLE

This is what separates amateurs from operators.

Show leadership 3 scenarios:
↳ Conservative: 20% engagement, 25% close rate
↳ Base case: 25% engagement, 30% close rate
↳ Aggressive: 35% engagement, 35% close rate

Map each scenario to pipeline and revenue ROI.

When leadership asks "what if it doesn't work?" you already have the answer.

STEP 5 // TIE TO EXISTING BENCHMARKS

Pull your historical data:
↳ What's your current cost-per-opportunity from other channels?
↳ What's your average CAC payback?
↳ What's your LTV:CAC ratio by segment?

Show how ABM compares. If your current CPO is $8K and ABM delivers at $7.1K, that's the story.

The pitch isn't "ABM is cool." The pitch is "ABM delivers pipeline at a lower CPO than our current mix."

Programs that launch with this model don't get cut at month 9.
They get expanded.

What did I miss?

comments.text:
Love this! Best ABM post I've read in a while, Ryan — the "decided before launch" thesis is exactly right, and Step 5's CPO reframe is the only pitch that survives a CFO.
 
Two things my finance partners always fire back that I'd fold in:
 
Time. Cost is a recurring monthly flow; pipeline is a lagged one-time number. With 6–12 month cycles, cash goes out now and revenue lands later — a J-curve. That trough is why programs get cut at month 9, before the revenue shows up. The model needs a period and a ramp, or it sets the exact expectation that kills it.
Incrementality. The math credits ABM with 100% of pipeline from those accounts, but some of those accounts would have closed anyway. The CFO killer question is "how do you know they wouldn't have converted without us?" A matched holdout group answers it and turns the whole model from correlation into causation.
 
Curious how you handle attribution when you present these — holdout, or something lighter?

The math only holds if the inputs are clean. How many of those 200 programs actually had engagement and close-rate data reconciled across the ad platform, CRM and ABM tool, versus someone eyeballing three dashboards and picking a number that felt right?
Ryan Carlin Most teams run ABM without knowing the unit economics. No cap table visibility means it dies the first time finance asks 'where's the ROI?'
ABM success metrics without inbox triage discipline produce vanity pipeline, not closed revenue.
Where is Sales in this analysis? If there’s no Sales and Marketing is only segmentation on steroids.
Decided before launch, not after, that's the whole trick. Most programs die because nobody wrote down what success meant on day one.
Great breakdown. The strongest ABM programs start with solid financial fundamentals clear economics make it much easier to measure, defend, and scale success.
Really helpful Ryan

Maybe 5 of 200 having a defensible cost model is the number that should get more attention than anything about the ABM tactics themselves - that's a 2.5% rate. Curious if that failure breaks down by company size: a $50M company's finance team usually forces this math whether marketing wants to or not, but a $10M company typically has nobody checking.

- Cons: Easy to undersold by people using the same mechanism

headline: I spend $6M/mo on Google ads
text: I spend $6M/mo on Google ads There are 4 types of incrementality studies you can run with them Brand Lift: → Survey-based test that measures whether the ad moved recall, awareness, consideration, favorability, or purchase intent → Runs on YouTube Video and Demand Gen campaigns → Needs $10,000 in spend over a 10-day window Search Lift: → Measures whether people searched for your brand after seeing the ad → Runs on the same Video and Demand Gen campaigns as Brand Lift → Rides alongside a Brand Lift study at no extra budget Conversion Lift based on users: → Splits your audience into people who saw the ad and a holdout who didn't → Native on Video and Demand Gen, needs a Google rep to set up on Search, Shopping, Display, or PMax → Gives directional results from $5,000 in spend and 1,000 conversions → Relies mostly on opt-in traffic, which brings its own measurement gaps Conversion Lift based on geography: → Splits regions on and off instead of individual users → Counts both online and offline conversions → Spans Search, Shopping, PMax, Video, Display, Demand Gen, and App → Needs a Google rep, and the geo split is noisier with no demographic breakdown Got $10,000 and 10 days? Run Brand Lift and Search Lift together. Got $5,000 and 1,000 conversions? Run Conversion Lift based on users. Need offline conversions counted? Run Conversion Lift based on geography. Note- a Google lift study is Google measuring Google. Pair the result with a holdout test of your own for greater impartiality. Hope this helps.

headline: Over the last 30 days, I've intentionally plummeted my LinkedIn impressions.
text: Over the last 30 days, I've intentionally plummeted my LinkedIn impressions. It's made my consulting business 10x easier to run and way simpler. Here's why: For context, I run a one person consulting business for agency CEOs who want to build authority and inbound from decision makers. We use LinkedIn as an attention platform because that's where a lot of my client's decision makers or their sphere of influence lives. For my own business, I have no real reason to get loads of impressions and neither do my client's businesses. More just means more shit to sift through. More connection requests, more profile views, more DMs etc. So, here's how I've intentionally plummeted my LinkedIn impressions so I can spend more time with the right people and less time actually on LinkedIn: 1. I write a post that's for a specific person I know my ICP very well. I've worked with nearly 100 agency founders and CEOs by now, over the last 5 years. I can switch it on or off when I want to talk to them. Recently I've turned that switch well and truly on. And my engagement and impressions have plummeted. If that didn't happen, then my strategy wouldn't be working. When you write a post for specific person, you create more impact with that specific person you're trying to reach. And you put off the people you don't want to spend time with. 2. I get profile views & connection requests Naturally from these posts, people click to see my profile. And if they think I'm giving them value, they could hit connect with me too. These are incredible signals of intent / interest in me and my business that I can make sales from. But if I've got a post that goes viral and I get 500 connection requests from it, I have to go through those and find the good ones. That can take hours / days. Same goes for profile views. So it makes zero sense to go viral for what I'm trying to do - speak to agency founders and CEOs who are doing $500k to $10M/year. 3. I talk to them If I have a shorter, more targeted list of people who have viewed my profile and connected with me, then it gives me less people to talk to. Less people to talk to = less time spent talking to people = more time getting results for my clients. And it also = more time with my 6 month old daughter and wife who are everything to me. When I talk to people, I make more money. So if I can talk to less people and talk to the right people, I'm using my time very efficiently. My client's need the same approach. Agency founders and CEOs are busy, running small teams and caring for their high profile clients. They don't need to waste time talking to freebie seekers. TL;DR: The opportunity you have on LinkedIn to find your exact ICP, is truly insane. Don't make it harder for yourself by attracting MORE people. Do everything you can to attract the RIGHT ones.

headline: Is one Google ad group taking ALL the spend?
text: Is one Google ad group taking ALL the spend? And NOT testing your other keywords? How to kickstart starved ad groups: 1. Rank and budget Search Lost IS (Rank): → If it's high, bids and quality score are the constraint. Fix those first. → If it's low, the starved ad group wins the auctions it enters. Search Lost IS (Budget): → If it's high, the campaign is capped. Raise the cap and the extra budget still flows to the dominant ad group. → If it's low, the campaign was never capped, and the starvation sits in how budget splits between ad groups. Either way, every ad group inherits the campaign's target CPA, and shared budget typically concentrates on the ad group with the deepest conversion history. 2. Fix the bid strategy first → Confirm the campaign runs Target CPA. Maximize Conversions gives no ad-group-level lever. → Raise the target CPA on the starved ad group. The override gives Smart Bidding permission to enter more auctions there, above the shared campaign default. → Raise the campaign budget cap next, so the ad group you unlocked doesn't get re-capped the moment it spends. 3. Overshoot the target CPA on purpose → On a low-spend ad group, set the target CPA above what you want, buying more auctions and more signal on what converts. → Pull the search term report while the overshoot runs and add negatives aggressively, or the spend lands on queries you don't want. Summary: → Check rank loss and budget loss together first → Switch the campaign to Target CPA → Raise the target on the starved ad group → Raise the campaign budget cap straight after → Add negatives while the overshoot runs A shared budget typically concentrates on the deepest conversion history by default. headline: I run a Meta/Google ads agency exclusively for (high) 8 & 9-figure brands.
text: I run a Meta / Google ads agency exclusively for (high) 8 & 9-figure brands. I'll be the first to say AEO is IMPORTANT. A quick 101 guide in case you haven't made any changes: 1. Map the buying decisions → A buying decision is anything a shopper settles before they buy, across discovery, comparison, objections, fit and care. → Pull 20-30 questions from support tickets, reviews, site search and post-purchase surveys, in the shopper's wording. → Example: "best polarized sunglasses for driving" (discovery), "[brand] vs [competitor]" (comparison), "is [brand] worth the price" (objection), "will [frames] fit a wide face" (fit), "how to clean [lenses]" (care). → Each question is a prompt. Type each prompt word for word into ChatGPT and Google AI Mode more than once. Log the answer, whether you were mentioned or cited, and which sources it pulled. 2. Fix eligibility → OpenAI runs 3 crawlers. GPTBot is training, OAI-SearchBot is search inclusion, ChatGPT-User is user-triggered fetches. → OpenAI will commit a felony (Hugging Face hack) for training; they may ignore your bots.txt , but I don’t risk it. A broad WAF rule or a wildcard disallow should in theory stop these bots which you don’t want. → Robots.txt changes take roughly 24 hours to register on OpenAI's side. 3. Build a product truth layer → Put price, availability, variants, shipping and returns in visible HTML. Keep your Merchant Center feed matching the page. → Same problem as a Meta catalog throwing disapprovals when the feed and the PDP disagree on price. Same fix, wider blast radius. 4. Publish data only you have → Publish return reasons, support questions, product tests and sizing failures. → This is the single most underused asset in DTC. Use it for AEO, but also for creative. 5. Answer the follow-up questions → AI Mode queries average 3x the length of a traditional search. → One decision page should cover the answer, trade-offs, edge cases and next step. 6. Write an honest comparison page → Own "X vs Y" with a dated methodology, named criteria, and who shouldn't buy your product. 7. Keep product names consistent → Use the same brand, model and variant names everywhere. Otherwise the engine reads your old reviews, new listing and current SKU as 3 unrelated things. 8. Earn corroboration → Fix wrong facts on the review sites and forum threads already showing up in your answers from move 1. 9. Land citations on the right page → Deep-link citations to the relevant PDP or guide. A great ad pointed at a generic homepage underperforms a mediocre ad pointed at the right page. 10. Measure → Track AI visibility in Search Console, AI referrals in analytics, and citation rates on your question set, dated before and after. → Add an AI option to your post-purchase survey. When someone asks an assistant and walks straight to your site, there's no click to capture. Shout out to Lorea Lastiri for this playbook. I'm not an AEO expert, but she is!

headline: 6 weeks ago, Google changed how bidding works
text: 6 weeks ago, Google changed how bidding works I checked 120 accounts to see what happened: CONTEXT - Before August 17, a budget-limited campaign with a $100 target CPA always tried to find the cheapest conversions. So if it ran out of budget it might have a CPA of $70. - Since August 17, Google bids up to the target CPA. So even if you run out of budget, you'll hit $100 CPA. - Target ROAS works the same way. A campaign beating its ROAS target gets pulled back down to the target. - Note: some of these 120 ad accounts we manage, some we don't. I split every campaign into three groups and compared 28 days before against 28 days after: 1. Budget-limited and beating target CPA 2. Budget-limited but already at target CPA 3. No target or no budget limit The campaigns that were budget-limited and beating target CPA - CPA up 63% - CPC up 20% - Conversions down 22% Campaigns that were budget-limited but already at target CPA: - CPA down 6% - CPC up 1% - Conversions down 1% The control group barely moved either: - CPC up 3% - CPA up 3% - Conversions down 1% What this means: If you're not actively managing your account, and ensuring you minimize Search Lost IS (Budget) by adjusting budgets and target CPA / ROAS, you will overpay for your conversions. (None of our client fit into this bucket) Hope this helps

comments.text: Interesting, but here’s another thing. Let’s say your tCPA is $100, the campaign is actually was over performing conversions at $80, and it’s Limited by Budget. You lower the tCPA to $80, but performance doesn’t stabilize. A lower tCPA means lower bids in the auctions. In theory, as you lower the tCPA, the Limited by Budget status should eventually disappear, since the number of conversions available at $80 or less is limited by demand. But it doesn’t. If the campaign remains Limited by Budget, simply adjusting the target to match actual performance doesn’t help maintain the previous results (before the update). And at that point, there’s no way to get back those overdelivering results you had before. So far, it looks like you either need to get out of Limited by Budget status (which often requires 2–3x your available budget) or switch to Maximize Conv. Value or Maximize Conversions, where maintaining your desired CPA/ROAS can be quite challenging.

headline: I tested Jev on negative Google ad keywords.
text: I tested Jev on negative Google ad keywords. Results are actually quite surprising. Jev is a new AI decision model that launched in early access on Sept 15. We tested it against a very mature AI workflow we have that identifies irrelevant keywords being bid for on Google ads and then removes them from campaigns. TEST: → Jev vs our tool (culmination of 2 years of iteration) → Jev and our tool each decided which search terms to block. → We scored both against a Claude review of every term. → Neither tool had context on the account outside of the website URL, to make it a fair read. Where Jev won → Jev caught 165 of the 292 junk terms. Our tool caught 39. → Jev cost $0.14 per 1,000 search terms. Our tool costs $2.68. Where Jev lost → Jev blocked 119 good search terms. Our tool blocked 35. → For every $1 of junk spend Jev removed, Jev blocked $2.60 of good spend. → Blocking a good term cuts off a source of leads which is worse than saving money. → Our tool marked 691 of 731 verdicts high confidence. Most of Jev's confidence scores sat between 0.2 and 0.6, close to a coin flip. Jev is cheap enough to try as a first-pass filter. But we're still keeping our search term tool. Has anyone else tested Jev on search terms yet?

text: This morning, I'm running a Sales team workshop on how to engage VP+ execs. A pic of Oprah, speaking at Harvard's 201 graduation ceremony, is my opening slide and story. Here's why. Oprah did 35,000+ interviews across her 25 years of hosting the Oprah Winfrey Show. Everyone from Beyonce, to Michael Jackson, Obama, George Bush, Whitney Houston, to Tom Cruise. In her speech, she spoke about the most important thing she learned after all of those years of interviewing celebrities and public figures. As soon as the camera went down, almost every guest asked some form of the same question. "Did what I say mean anything?" Presidents. Celebrities. The most famous of the famous. All of them cared about feeling seen, heard and understood. In Sales, we have this tendency to put executives on a pedestal. We think of them as figures, not people. We flex our biggest vocabulary. We speak in dry business language. Yet, they're the same people who drank 4 beers while watching the Brewers win last night (GO BREW CREW). The same people who spent the weekend cheering on the sidelines for their kid's basketball team. The same people who have 32,372 photos of their dog on their camera roll. The same people who have hobbies and nicknames their friends gave them. And, the same people who posted on LinkedIn and get 11 likes. Or, who write an article that they're worried no one saw or read. Or, who had a major career win that they're proud of. Execs are no different than Oprah's guests. They value being seen, heard, and understood. ESPECIALLY when it's clear that you, a human, put thought into them. Not an AI bot. They can almost always tell. I've always been a believer that the best sellers are pretty damn good marketers, too. Because if you want to stand out to a VP+ exec - you have to stand out amidst the 1000 other sellers who want their attention, too. Being memorable matters.

headline: Google ads over holidays periods can suck.
text: Google ads over holidays periods can suck. How to forecast performance & adjust bids in advance. 1. Holidays carry CVR risk → Traffic changes over holiday periods. B2B search volume thins out over Thanksgiving week and between Christmas and New Year because buyers are off work. Retail volume spikes into Black Friday and Cyber Monday, then drops off. → Volume on its own doesn't hurt CPA, since you pay per click and Google bids per auction. People keep clicking but delay the purchase, so the drop lands in conversion rate first. → Smart Bidding sets each bid from auction signals and accounts for conversion delay. A sharp CVR drop over a few days can land before bids catch up, and you pay pre-holiday prices for holiday clicks. → E.g. a hypothetical account at a $10 CPC and 5% CVR runs a $200 CPA. If CVR slips to 4% over a 4-day holiday weekend and CPC holds, CPA comes in at $250 for those 4 days. → Holding a $200 CPA on a 4% CVR takes an $8 CPC. A -20% conversion rate adjustment pushes bids toward that $8 but doesn't guarantee a 20% lower CPC. Set the change ahead of the window, through the seasonality adjustment in step 2 or a manual bid cut on campaigns that don't use Smart Bidding. 2. Seasonality adjustments for short windows → A seasonality adjustment tells Smart Bidding ahead of time that conversion rates will move over a set date range. → Don't set a seasonality adjustment for every holiday. Smart Bidding already accounts for normal seasonality. Use the adjustment for a significant, short-lived CVR change you have a reason to expect. → Find it under the Tools icon, then Budgets and bidding, then Adjustments, then the Seasonal tab. Hit the plus button and pick Conversion rate. → Set the start and end dates, choose which campaigns it covers, and enter the conversion rate change you expect. For the hypothetical 5% to 4% drop above, enter -20%. → Keep the adjustment to events of 1 to 7 days. Google says seasonality adjustments may be less effective over longer periods. → The adjustment reverts automatically once the end date passes. 3. Read lag before reacting → Conversion lag is the gap between the click you pay for and the conversion Google reports against it. A form fill lands the same day. A signed deal can take weeks. → Holidays stretch that gap. People click on the Wednesday and buy after the long weekend. B2B buyers click before the break and convert once the office reopens. → E.g. the 4% CVR in the hypothetical above can be understated. Conversions from holiday clicks get reported after the weekend and the 4% climbs. → Pull your time-to-conversion report before the window (Goals, then Measurement, then Attribution) so you know how long your lag runs. → Wait out that lag before judging the holiday week. Hope this helps.

headline: Most brands running Meta traffic to Amazon are optimizing for the wrong person.
text: Most brands running Meta traffic to Amazon are optimizing for the wrong person. You can't fire a purchase event from Amazon back to Meta. So the campaign optimizes on the last thing it can see: the outbound click. Meta gets very good at finding people who click Amazon links. It has no idea which of them ever bought. I've managed $150M+ in Meta spend and this is the worst signal environment I deal with. Was talking through this with the founders at Jurni , who was willing to share some data on their learnings. Jurni's fix is a "Pre-retail landing experience" sitting between the ad and the PDP. What the page has to do: 1. Continue the ad, don't restart it. Same hook, same visual, same claim. If the page reintroduces the brand, you've reset the sale. 2. Handle the objection the PDP can't. On Amazon you're one tile in a grid of 40 competitors. The page is the only place you control the comparison. 3. One exit. No nav, no footer, no second offer. One button, deep linked to the right variant and pack size. Across their beauty and CPG customer set: - CPA down ~19% - ROAS up ~26% - 22% of ad traffic never clicks through to Amazon That third number is the one people react badly to. A fifth of your traffic dies on the page. That's the point though. That's low intent traffic getting filtered before it costs you an Amazon session. And now you have two segments you never had: people who clicked through, and people who didn't. Fire the first as your optimization event. Then it compounds. Higher-intent traffic on the PDP lifts conversion rate, and Amazon's ranking rewards conversion rate. You buy better traffic, and the algorithm hands you cheaper organic placement for it. Worth noting- these pages Jurni builds are AI-generated per-audience/per-ad variant, not one static page. That's part of why the objection-handling can be this specific: each version is built to match the exact ad it's continuing, and they're tracking performance per variant, not just in aggregate Caveat: this is their data across their customers, not mine, and CPA is in-platform. I'd want to see it hold in a geo test before I called it incremental.

headline: This Claude skill audits your Google Ads agency.
text: This Claude skill audits your Google Ads agency. I built it to audit $6M/mo of our own Google spend. 1. Account coverage → Lists every child account it can read, with currency, timezone and conversion definitions. → Flags zero-spend accounts and any account missing from Google's change log. → Treats the MCC as a directory. Spend gets pulled from each account directly. 2. Actuals vs dated forecast → Pulls the forecast the agency agreed before the period started. Spend, qualified volume, unit cost. → Compares mature results against that forecast on matched dates and conversion definitions. → Excludes recent cohorts that haven't finished converting. → Reports "forecast unavailable" if none exists and compares to a mature prior period instead. 3. Change log vs needed work → Names the constraint in the account first. Measurement, intent, economics, creative or capacity. → Splits every logged change into human edits, API and script activity, and auto-applied recommendations. → Lines up the changes made against the changes the account needed. E.g. if spend has no reliable conversions, the log should show tracking work before bid changes. → Ignores edit count as a score. 74% of the 57,275 changes across 44 of our accounts last month were bulk negative keywords. 4. Grades per area → Grades measurement, business performance, prioritization, change quality and follow-through separately. → Four grades. Supported, Needs review, Action required, or Cannot evaluate. → Refuses to use optimization score, ad strength, keyword count or campaign count as evidence. → Returns a read-only report with recommendations. It never applies changes. You know what to do to get it PLUS - made this video with Opus 5.5 in one shot. What do you think?

comments.text: the shift from measuring activity to measuring whether the right problem was addressed is powerful. automation should improve decisions, not just increase the number of actions

The measurement grade will mark down agencies doing the right work, because most tracking fixes never touch the Google Ads change log. A repaired purchase tag ships as a GTM container version, server-side tagging runs in its own container, and offline conversion uploads come through the CRM, so an account with no reliable conversions can look like it only got bid edits. Pulling GTM version history and GA4 admin change history onto the same timeline as the Ads log is what lets that tracking step get graded at all.

Naming the constraint first is the right order, and I'd check measurement before the other four because every later check depends on it. In an account I audited recently, page visits were set as primary lead conversions, so the numbers looked better than the real calls and bookings. Listing conversion definitions per account is a good start. Confirming each primary one is a real outcome is what makes the rest of the audit trustworthy.
The strongest part is refusing to reward activity for its own sake. Change volume means little if it doesn’t address the account’s constraint. Adam Treboutat

headline: We ran a direct mail campaign that generated 4,600 leads and 450 opportunities for a $1,500 offer.
text: We ran a direct mail campaign that generated 4,600 leads and 450 opportunities for a $1,500 offer. How you can too Results: → Roughly 375,000 mail pieces sent over the program → About 4,600 leads → About 450 campaign-attributed opportunities, roughly 1 in 10 leads → Roughly $1M in influenced pipeline 1. Audiences → We split the list into four audiences, the house file, previous responders, competitor audiences, and intent-based prospect lists. → Each audience got its own drop and its own campaign in Salesforce so we could compare cost per opportunity head to head. → House file and previous responders came in cheaper per opportunity than the broad prospect lists. → A previous responder had already replied to the brand once, so the piece read as a follow-up. 2. Tracking → Every piece carried a mailer-specific URL, a QR code, and UTM tags. → Salesforce logged the campaign attribution on every lead that came through a mailer link. → We matched back CRM records for responders who came in through another channel after the piece landed. → A QR scan alone does not tell you whether a piece acquired a customer profitably, so every audience was judged on cost per opportunity after the same maturation window. 3. Mailer creative and offer → We send a handwritten style letter for a B2B offer as we tend to see higher conversion rates versus a postcard. → We adjust copy by segment. For example, a previous responder gets a reminder of what they looked at before, and a competitor list audience member gets a switching offer. → Every piece carries one offer and one call to action. The reader scans the QR code or types the short URL. Summary: → Split the list by audience type and track each one on its own campaign. → Put a URL, QR code, and UTM on every piece and matchback the rest. → Judge audiences on cost per opportunity after the same window. → Put one offer and one call to action on a letter written to the segment. Hope this helps

comments.text: Splitting out audiences like that really does make a difference. I’ve seen tailored creative outperform generic every time, especially when it references their previous interactions or interests.
Really interesting breakdown Adam. The tracking part is especially important. Getting leads is one thing, but knowing which audience actually turns into opportunities is the real insight.
